title: Physical reservoir computing with nonlinear temperature characteristics of thermal conductivity
abstract: Physical reservoir computing (PRC) has emerged as a low-cost machine-learning framework for edge computing applications, where real-time processing and energy efficiency are critical due to the rapid growth of data generated by Internet-of-Things devices. This study proposes a PRC scheme based on nonlinear heat-conduction phenomena arising from the nonlinear temperature-dependent thermal conductivity of materials and examines its computational properties using a one-dimensional model. Information is encoded as transient thermal inputs applied at one boundary, while the resulting temporal temperature responses at multiple spatial positions constitute the reservoir states. Nondimensionalization of the governing heat equation reveals key dimensionless parameters that govern dynamical memory and nonlinearity, enabling systematic exploration of the design space independent of specific physical units. Performance is evaluated using benchmark tasks, including the short-term memory task and the parity check task. The results demonstrate that memory capacity and nonlinear transformation capability can be tuned by adjusting the heat-input magnitude and the thermal diffusion time scale. The proposed heat-conduction-based PRC successfully performs both benchmark tasks, demonstrating the feasibility of implementing PRC through nonlinear thermal transport in materials with temperature-dependent thermal conductivity. These findings indicate that engineered thermal media can serve as effective physical reservoirs with material-level tunability for energy-efficient computing systems.

title: You Can't Prefer Emotions You Don't Sample: Intensity Undershoot in DPO-Tuned LLMs
abstract: Ask a language model to respond "very excitedly," and its output is typically only mildly more energetic. We quantify this effect. We condition an instruction-tuned LLM on a continuous Valence-Arousal (VA) target, where valence measures how pleasant a state is and arousal how activated it is, measure the achieved affect with a frozen regressor, and sweep the requested target from -1 to +1. The response moves far less than asked: the gain, the slope of achieved against requested affect, is only 0.26 for valence and 0.13 for arousal on Llama-3.1-8B, where a faithful controller would score 1. The model systematically undershoots requested emotional intensity, which puts a number on the qualitative observation of Fazzi et al. (2025). Our experiments trace this to the preference-learning pipeline. Training targets from natural corpora such as EmoBank are neutral-heavy, and the sampled candidates themselves rarely reach extreme affect, so Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is left with no extreme exemplar to prefer. If instead we cover the target space uniformly and sample a hotter, larger candidate pool, valence gain rises from 0.26 to 0.40 +/- 0.02 (3 seeds) and extrapolation error drops, at only a modest in-distribution cost (EmoBank-test VA distance 0.092 to 0.107). The same recipe reproduces on Qwen3-8B (gain_v 0.44, with in-distribution accuracy preserved). Arousal is harder and less reliable: its gain barely moves on average and swings across seeds (0.14 +/- 0.07, against valence's tight +/- 0.02), because raising arousal needs candidates the base model is reluctant to generate. The evidence indicates that faithful intensity is bottlenecked by the extremity of the candidate pool rather than by the conditioning format.

title: Experimental realization of quantum-computing-enhanced sensing
abstract: Quantum algorithms offer computational advantages, yet incorporating them into quantum sensing and converting these advantages into enhanced information acquisition remains challenging. Here, we realize quantum-computing-enhanced sensing in a spin-oscillator architecture, where a microwave cavity provides a high-dimensional quantum register and a coupled superconducting qubit serves as the sensor. The unknown signal directly generates the phase oracle operation, establishing a natural physical interface between quantum computation and sensing. We experimentally demonstrate the first Grover search in a bosonic mode and observe quantum amplitude amplification in a Hilbert space spanning more than 128 photons. For the same number of sensing iterations, our protocol extracts more information and resolves more frequency candidates than classical sequential search. Our results establish signal-driven oracles as a route for harnessing oracle-based quantum algorithms and realizing quantum-computing-enhanced sensing.

title: Topologically Consistent Agricultural Parcel Vectorization with Semantic-Guided Diffusion and Topology-Aware Polygonization
abstract: Agricultural parcel polygons play a fundamental role in geospatial applications such as precision agriculture, land administration, and crop monitoring. Beyond regular polygon geometry and low vertex redundancy, practical parcel maps should avoid topological conflicts and preserve common boundaries between adjacent fields. Yet this requirement remains largely unresolved: segmentation-based methods mainly produce parcel masks or raster boundary cues and rely on heuristic raster-to-vector conversion, instance- and contour-based methods reconstruct parcels independently, and recent vector-oriented methods improve polygon regularity but do not explicitly recover adjacent parcels from a shared topological structure. To address this gap, we propose a semantic-guided diffusion framework for topologically consistent agricultural parcel vectorization. It couples joint edge--vertex latent diffusion with supervised multi-cue conditioning to generate geometrically regularised parcel-boundary and vertex primitives while suppressing false-positive responses. A topology-aware parcel polygon reconstruction method then converts these primitives into regular polygons by reconstructing parcel faces from a common planar graph, enabling adjacent predicted parcels to reuse shared boundaries and avoid mutual interior intrusion. Extensive experiments on the AI4SmallFarms and iFLYTEK datasets evaluate parcel vectorization in terms of pixel-level coverage, geometric fidelity, object-level correctness, and topological consistency. The results show strong and competitive performance, with zero measured intrusion ratio and the highest shared-edge recall, demonstrating the potential of the proposed framework for accurate, regular, and topologically consistent agricultural parcel vectorization.

title: Joint-Conditioned Stereo Surface Reasoning for Interaction Field Estimation
abstract: Predicting hand--object interaction fields requires locating the nearest object-surface point for each hand joint, often from small and partially occluded image regions. We view this task as joint-conditioned surface-endpoint estimation: each joint has its own nearest endpoint, while endpoints from the same hand can draw on shared local surface evidence. This structure motivates Joint-Conditioned Stereo Surface Reasoning (JSSR). A temporal-stereo network jointly predicts 3D joints, a direct interaction field, and per-view endpoint evidence. Calibrated candidate search evaluates endpoint hypotheses using joint-specific image compatibility and cross-view correspondence. A hand-shared candidate support lets joints draw on common surface evidence, and a learned residual gate controls the geometric correction when observations are ambiguous. Our system built on this method ranked third on the SHOW3D Interaction Field Challenge leaderboard.

title: A Performance-Security Balanced Framework for Lightweight Cryptography Incorporating Hardware Acceleration and Adaptive Key Exchange in IoT Environments
abstract: The rapid growth of the Internet of Things (IoT) has intensified the demand for lightweight cryptography that can secure billions of resource-constrained devices without prohibitive costs in energy or latency. This paper proposes a performance–security balanced framework that specifies (i) an adaptive key exchange protocol based on X25519 with HKDF-SHA256, (ii) authenticated encryption using ChaCha20-Poly1305 or AES-GCM with strict nonce/counter management, and (iii) hardware acceleration on ARM Cortex-M4 and FPGA modules to reduce computation and energy overhead. Protocol message flows, nonce/rekey rules, and full test vectors are provided to ensure reproducibility. Experimental evaluation on structured IoT traffic datasets shows that hardware-assisted AEAD achieves up to 38% lower encryption latency and 29% reduced energy consumption compared to software-only baselines. Security validation includes formal arguments, replay/MITM/downgrade attack experiments, and side-channel leakage assessment (TVLA), all of which confirm robustness against the defined threat model. The resulting framework offers a quantifiable and reproducible approach to securing IoT infrastructures in domains such as healthcare, smart cities, industrial networks, and intelligent transportation systems.

title: Title: Quantum-Enhanced Fractal Complexity via Entangled States
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of quantum entanglement to enhance fractal complexity, offering a novel approach to generating intricate and unpredictable structures. We introduce a "Quantum Entanglement Gradient" algorithm designed to dynamically modulate entanglement within fractal elements, fostering a self-organizing process leading to increased complexity. The core mechanism leverages the inherent properties of entangled quantum states to overcome the limitations of classical computational approaches in modeling and generating fractal patterns. This research explores the feasibility of utilizing quantum entanglement as a transformative tool for materials science and computational design, potentially leading to advancements in areas such as data visualization, image synthesis, and the creation of novel physical phenomena. The paper details the algorithm's implementation, initial results, and discusses future research directions.

title: 基于动态自适应的随机梯度下降算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel randomized incremental descent (RIDS) algorithm, termed "Dynamic Adaptive Random Gradient Descent" (DARDS), designed to enhance optimization performance through dynamic adjustment of learning rate and step size. Traditional random gradient descent struggles with noisy data and non-convex landscapes, often leading to suboptimal solutions. DARDS addresses these challenges by incorporating a dynamically adjustable learning rate and step size mechanism. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through extensive testing on a variety of machine learning tasks, showcasing significant improvements in convergence speed, solution quality, and robustness to parameter variations. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop that continuously monitors the error signal and adjusts the learning rate and step size to guide the algorithm towards optimal parameters.

This approach offers a significant advancement in quantum state analysis, providing a more comprehensive and efficient method for investigating and interpreting quantum systems. This paper details the algorithm's design, implementation, and preliminary results, demonstrating its potential to revolutionize quantum state analysis.

title: Dynamic Topology Network Learning (DTNL)
abstract: This paper presents Dynamic Topology Network Learning (DTNL), a novel approach to network design inspired by the dynamic topology of biological neural networks. DTNL employs a biologically-inspired agent-based modeling framework where individual nodes, mimicking neurons, possess sensing, decision-making, and actuation capabilities. These nodes communicate via simulated synaptic connections, and the network topology dynamically adapts based on interactions and feedback mechanisms, including node addition/deletion and connection strength adjustments. The core claim is that by simulating the dynamic topology of biological neural networks, we can construct a computational network capable of adapting its structure to changing environments. This approach aims to achieve more flexible and adaptive network architectures compared to traditional static network configurations. The key mechanism revolves around agent-based modeling and dynamic adjustments to optimize network performance.

title: Distributed Federated Learning with Differential Privacy for Medical Data
abstract: This paper investigates the application of distributed federated learning (DFL) combined with differential privacy (DP) to address the pressing need for privacy-preserving collaborative model training in the medical domain. The core challenge lies in leveraging the collective intelligence of decentralized medical datasets without compromising the sensitive patient information contained within. We propose a novel framework that integrates DFL with DP, specifically focusing on adding calibrated noise to model updates during the training process. This mechanism effectively limits the influence of any single patient's data, mitigating the risk of re-identification and ensuring compliance with stringent privacy regulations like HIPAA. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated through a theoretical analysis and a conceptual design, highlighting its potential to unlock the value of distributed medical data while safeguarding patient confidentiality. The key innovation rests in the adaptive noise scaling strategy, which balances privacy guarantees with model accuracy. The results indicate a viable path towards building robust and trustworthy federated learning systems for medical applications.

title: Self-Correcting Neural Networks via Relational Memory
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to designing self-correcting neural networks by integrating a relational memory module with a recurrent neural network. Traditional backpropagation relies on error signals flowing backward through the network, which can be inefficient and prone to vanishing gradients. Our method proposes a proactive self-improvement mechanism where the network actively learns from its own mistakes by storing and utilizing input-output relationships within a relational memory. This memory module dynamically updates connections based on observed errors, allowing the network to refine its internal representations and improve its predictive accuracy without relying solely on gradient-based optimization. The core claim is that neural networks can be designed to self-correct their internal representations through a relational memory. The core mechanism involves integrating a recurrent neural network with a separate relational memory module. We demonstrate, theoretically and conceptually, the feasibility and potential advantages of this approach, highlighting its ability to address limitations of standard backpropagation.

title: Understanding the Impact of Model Pruning on Long-Tail Forgetting and Explanation Reliability in Medical Imaging
abstract: Model pruning is widely used to compress deep neural networks, reducing memory and computational requirements with minimal impact on aggregate performance. However, its effect on model behavior remains poorly understood, particularly for long-tailed medical datasets where rare but clinically important conditions are underrepresented. Furthermore, it remains unclear whether pruned models preserve reliable explanations of their predictions. To address this gap, we present a systematic study of long-tail forgetting and explanation reliability under model pruning. Across two long-tailed medical imaging datasets, two CNN architectures, four pruning methods, and sparsity levels up to 95\%, we evaluate predictive performance, explanation stability, and explanation faithfulness. Our results show that predictive performance exhibits a strong frequency-dependent trend, with lower-frequency classes generally experiencing earlier and larger degradation than higher-frequency classes. In contrast, explanation stability and faithfulness are influenced primarily by the pruning strategy, with gradient-informed methods preserving explanation reliability more effectively under aggressive compression. Qualitative and mechanistic analyses further indicate that explanation degradation is primarily associated with the collapse of class-discriminative gradients rather than the disappearance of feature activations. These findings suggest that model compression should be evaluated beyond aggregate performance. Incorporating class-aware and explanation-aware evaluation reveals failure modes that would otherwise remain hidden, while moderate sparsity levels provide a practical balance between compression, predictive performance, and explanation reliability.

title: PICANet: Physics-Informed Cascaded Asymmetric Network for Infrared Small Target Detection
abstract: Infrared small target detection (ISTD) is an important research direction in image processing. However, existing methods are limited by severe background noise propagation and target degradation in high-level semantic features. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a plug-and-play physics-informed cascaded asymmetric network, named PICANet. Specifically, we construct a hierarchical prior decoupling module to explicitly extract low-level and high-level physical information, thereby characterizing target features at different levels rather than relying solely on convolutional extraction. title: Protocol effects on feature-based hardware-Trojan detection across Trust-Hub families
abstract: Trust-Hub reuses host circuits: several files differ mainly in the inserted Trojan. When gates from sibling variants enter both training and test folds, a detector can benefit from host logic it has already seen. We measure that effect instead of proposing another classifier. The corpus contains 49,124 gates from 16 netlists grouped into five host families. We left the parser, 36 gate features, class weighting, model settings, threshold, and family-level aggregation unchanged and altered one choice: the test boundary. The three settings draw test gates from the pooled corpus, withhold a complete netlist, or withhold every variant of one host. The choice matters. Random forest records F1/AP of 0.914/0.978 with pooled gates, 0.636/0.851 with one netlist held out, and 0.460/0.577 with a host family held out. XGBoost falls from 0.946/0.976 to 0.464/0.544 across the same comparison. Logistic regression loses AP, although its fixed-threshold F1 is not monotonic. Each family shows the same pooled-to-family direction. Feature removal, repeated model and simulator seeds, score normalization, parser-related exclusions, and a smaller sample change the size of the gap without reversing it. Aggregation also matters: a gate-weighted average is dominated by the larger ISCAS files, so the headline values give each host family one vote. Bootstrap and jackknife summaries keep the gap positive, but their folds reuse training families. We treat the five family rows as descriptive evidence rather than independent trials. Five host families are too few for a population claim, and the experiment says nothing about transfer to a new cell library or an industrial design. It supports a narrower conclusion: sibling benchmark variants can inflate apparent transfer. Benchmarks with several variants of one host circuit should report family-aware holdouts and all five family results beside pooled scores.

title: A Secure Multilingual Knowledge Extraction Pipeline for Virtual Collaboration Using Generative AI
abstract: The move to working from home and mixing office work with homework has caused meetings where people speak languages. These meetings have transcripts that include company details. These transcripts are usually not recorded, summarized or stored safely so they can be used in languages. Previous research focused on making summaries translating, keeping information secure and following GDPR rules. There was no solution. This paper describes the design and testing of a system that finds and removes information identifies who spoke makes summaries and translates all while keeping GDPR rules in mind inside a Streamlit application. When I tested the system on a transcript with speakers, I got speaker detection with a score of 1.000 and clear summaries in all languages. The evaluation scores were ROUGE-1 0.386 ROUGE-2 0.207 ROUGE-L 0.341 and BLEU 7.07. However, some evaluation metrics were not correct: the average F1 score was, outside the expected range. The historical dashboard showed NaN values for precision and recall. These problems mean that even though the system works for language processing and functions the security and metric validation parts still need to be improved before the system can claim to be fully compliant.

title: The impact of Artificial Intelligence on Modern Business Management
abstract: Artificial Intelligence has emerged as one of the most powerful technological phenomena in shaping modern business management. Artificial intelligence systems nowadays can analyze enormous amounts of data, create content, help with complex decision-making, personalize customer communications, forecast market trends, and carry out multi-step tasks with little to no human intervention, whereas earlier information technologies were primarily created to automate repetitive processes. As a result, AI is altering not just the activities but also the foundations of marketing, finance, human resource management, leadership, organization design, management, and strategic decision-making. This article explores how AI is affecting contemporary company management by looking at its potential, uses, difficulties, and consequences for managerial practice in the future. This piece is intellectual and grounded on literature. It makes use of known management literature, scholarly research, and study on international policy. The article concludes by proposing a human-centered AI management framework based on strategic alignment, data readiness, workforce capability, responsible governance, continuous evaluation, and organizational transformation.

title: Detecting Display-Affinity-Based Screen Capture Evasion on Windows
abstract: The Windows API function SetWindowDisplayAffinity, combined with the WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE flag, allows an application to render a window that is fully visible to the local user while being invisible to screenshot tools, screen recorders, and screen-sharing software. Originally introduced in Windows 7 to protect sensitive on-screen content such as password prompts, this mechanism has recently drawn attention as a plausible technical basis for a wave of "undetectable" AI-assisted overlay tools marketed for use in job interviews and online examinations. Public reporting on these tools is inconsistent and largely unverified with respect to their internal implementation. Rather than claim to detect any specific commercial product, this work studies the underlying, documented Windows mechanism itself: we present the design, implementation, and empirical evaluation of a lightweight, open-source detector that enumerates visible windows and flags any window marked with WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE. The detector is implemented in Node.js using FFI bindings to the Win32 API, packaged as a Windows tray application, and evaluated against a purpose-built test harness that reproduces the evasion technique. We verify empirically that a window using this flag is absent from both a native Windows screenshot and a live Google Meet screen share, while remaining visible to and correctly flagged by our detector in real time, with no false positives observed among ordinary application windows during testing. We discuss the scope and limitations of a single-technique detector, situate it against existing detection approaches, and outline directions for future work.

title: Title: Adaptive Dimension Scaling Algorithm: A Theoretical Framework
abstract: This paper presents a theoretical framework for adaptive dimension scaling algorithms, aiming to establish a robust and automated method for parameter tuning. The core focus is to build a theoretical framework that explains the effectiveness of dimension scaling algorithms across diverse data distributions and model parameter settings. A novel algorithm is proposed that dynamically adjusts dimension scaling parameters based on a theoretical model, mitigating the risk of over-scaling. The study explores how incorporating a theoretical model can guide the dimension scaling process, leading to optimized model performance. The paper introduces a mechanism for automated parameter adjustment, emphasizing the importance of a solid theoretical foundation. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of dimension scaling, offering a practical approach to improve algorithm efficiency.

title: Title: Adaptive Topology for Semantic Networks
abstract: This paper explores the application of adaptive topology to semantic networks, aiming to address the inherent limitations of current representations. Semantic networks, while valuable for knowledge representation and reasoning, often suffer from brittleness – meaning their structure is easily disrupted by minor changes in the input. We propose a novel system, the Adaptive Topology Engine, designed to dynamically adjust the network's structure, ensuring robustness and enhanced informativeness through continuous refinement. This system leverages a feedback loop, constantly evaluating the network's integrity and adjusting the topology to maintain optimal performance. The core mechanism centers around a continuous re-evaluation of node and relationship connections, driven by a dynamic weighting system. The paper details the architecture, the algorithm's components, and the evaluation metrics used to demonstrate the system's effectiveness. We showcase the system's ability to handle complex scenarios involving varying input data and demonstrate a significant improvement in network resilience compared to static topology methods. Furthermore, we explore the theoretical implications of the adaptive approach, considering the stability and convergence properties of the system.

title: Probability Geometric Optimization Algorithm with Dynamic Adaptability
abstract: This paper introduces a novel probability geometric optimization algorithm incorporating dynamic adaptability. Traditional optimization methods often rely on static parameter adjustments, limiting their effectiveness in complex problems. We propose a dynamic adaptivity mechanism that allows the algorithm to dynamically adjust its parameter range based on real-time data point analysis. This approach enhances convergence speed and improves the generalization ability of the optimization process. The core of this design is a mechanism that evaluates data points and adjusts the parameter space in response to these evaluations, enabling the algorithm to efficiently navigate the search space. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm through extensive numerical experiments on a series of challenging optimization problems.

title: Quantum-Inspired Randomized Search for Optimization Landscapes
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to randomized search algorithms, termed Quantum-Inspired Randomized Search (QIRS). The core idea is to leverage principles from quantum mechanics, specifically probabilistic amplitude assignment, to enhance the efficiency of the search process. Traditional randomized search methods often struggle with complex, multi-dimensional optimization landscapes, frequently converging to local optima. QIRS addresses this by assigning probabilities to potential solutions based on their similarity to the current best solution. These probabilities are then dynamically adjusted based on observed performance, creating a more adaptive and potentially more effective search strategy. The methodology is presented with a detailed explanation of the algorithm and its underlying principles. Empirical results (although not presented through experimental data) demonstrate the potential benefits of this approach, suggesting that quantum-inspired techniques can significantly improve the performance of randomized search algorithms, particularly in scenarios with high dimensionality and complex landscapes. The key contribution lies in the direct application of probabilistic amplitude assignment, a concept borrowed from quantum mechanics, within the context of randomized search.

title: Pulse Adaptive Quantum Computing: A Topological Approach to Quantum Entanglement
abstract: Quantum computing holds the promise of revolutionary advancements across diverse fields, from drug discovery and materials science to cryptography and artificial intelligence. However, achieving robust and scalable quantum computation requires meticulous control over quantum states, particularly entanglement. Traditional methods often struggle to precisely manipulate entanglement, leading to decoherence and errors. This paper investigates a novel approach to quantum entanglement – Pulse Adaptive Quantum Computing (PAQC) – leveraging dynamic pulse adjustments to enhance entanglement strength and stability. We propose a mechanism where pulses are dynamically modulated to subtly shift the entanglement's characteristics, ultimately improving the fidelity and efficiency of quantum information transfer. The core claim is that PAQC offers a significant improvement over current entanglement control techniques through dynamic adjustment and precision. This work presents a theoretical framework and preliminary experimental validation demonstrating the potential of this technique to address key challenges in quantum information processing.

title: Title: Non-Local Topology Analysis using Graph Neural Networks
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for analyzing topology across large, distributed graphs, aiming to reveal hidden patterns and relationships. Traditional topological analysis methods often struggle with scalability, limiting their applicability to complex real-world datasets. We propose a novel GNN architecture specifically designed to handle these challenges, incorporating a mechanism to effectively capture long-range dependencies. The core of this work involves a deep learning model that learns to represent graph structures and then utilizes this representation to identify subtle topological features. The system is engineered to scale to significantly larger graphs than existing methods, offering a substantial improvement in the scope and depth of topological insights. This research contributes to the field of graph representation and topology analysis by demonstrating a practical approach to overcoming the limitations of existing techniques. The primary goal is to produce a robust and scalable system capable of uncovering previously unnoticed topological relationships within extensive graph networks.

title: Quantum Parallel Matrix Multiplication Leveraging Quantum State Superposition
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to accelerating matrix multiplication by exploiting the principles of quantum state superposition. The core idea centers on decomposing the matrix multiplication process into a series of quantum state superposition calculations and leveraging quantum interference effects for enhanced computational speed. Traditional parallel matrix multiplication algorithms primarily rely on classical computation methods, often failing to effectively harness the inherent parallel processing capabilities of quantum hardware. This work presents a quantum algorithm designed specifically to address this limitation. The algorithm utilizes the superposition of quantum states to perform multiple matrix multiplication operations concurrently. The mathematical framework is presented, detailing the quantum gate sequence and the overall computational flow. The potential for significant speedup is discussed, acknowledging the challenges inherent in realizing such an algorithm on current and near-term quantum devices. The key contribution lies in the direct mapping of matrix multiplication onto a quantum system, optimizing for superposition and interference. The theoretical analysis provides a foundation for future research and development in this area.

title: Quantum Computing-Based Cryptographic Key Distribution Protocol Optimization
abstract: This paper investigates the optimization of cryptographic key distribution protocols utilizing the capabilities of quantum computing. Traditional key distribution protocols often rely on classical mathematical models which are vulnerable to attacks from future quantum computers. This research proposes a novel approach that leverages quantum simulation to analyze and refine these protocols. Specifically, we explore the use of quantum computers to simulate various attacks targeting key distribution schemes, enabling a more thorough assessment of their security. The results of these simulations guide the optimization of the protocols, leading to potentially more robust and secure key exchange mechanisms. This work contributes to the emerging field of post-quantum cryptography by directly addressing the vulnerabilities of existing protocols through a quantum-informed analytical framework. The core claim of this research is to enhance the security of key distribution through the simulation capabilities of quantum computers. The central mechanism involves simulating attacks on existing protocols to evaluate their vulnerabilities and inform protocol optimization. ---

title: Self-Supervised Learning of Hierarchical Feature Representations from Video Streams
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to self-supervised learning for video data, driven by the inherent hierarchical structure present within video streams. We propose a model architecture designed to learn robust feature representations by predicting future frames from past frames. The core of our method utilizes recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and attention mechanisms to effectively capture temporal dependencies and build hierarchical relationships within the video data. Unlike existing self-supervised methods that often treat video as a sequence of independent frames, our approach explicitly models the temporal order and hierarchical structure, leading to a more effective and efficient learning process. The resulting feature representations demonstrate superior performance in downstream tasks compared to methods that do not incorporate this hierarchical perspective. We detail the model architecture, training methodology, and evaluation results, highlighting the advantages of our self-supervised learning framework.

title: Core Claim: Develop a dynamic topology framework for high-order matrix evolution, enabling the understanding and optimization of complex non-linear matrix topology, thereby facilitating more efficient machine learning models.
abstract: The study of complex non-linear matrix topology is crucial for various applications in machine learning, particularly in areas such as dimensionality reduction and feature learning. Traditional approaches often rely on static representations and optimization techniques, limiting the ability to effectively capture the intricate dynamics of these structures. This paper introduces a novel dynamic topology framework for high-order matrix evolution, aiming to improve the efficiency and adaptability of machine learning models. The framework utilizes a dynamic matrix evolution process directly linked to topology changes, offering a paradigm shift towards intelligent and automated topology adjustment. We propose a new method for representing and manipulating matrix transformations, which can be effectively utilized in optimization and model training. This research addresses a critical challenge in machine learning: the need for robust and adaptive methods to handle complex, non-linear data. The core mechanism focuses on creating a framework that dynamically adjusts the matrix's topology, providing improved interpretability and performance. This work demonstrates the potential of this approach through simulations and preliminary analysis, suggesting significant improvements in model training and optimization.

title: DIFFERENTIAL EFFECTIVENESS OF STOP VS. SHIFT INSTRUCTIONS IN THE IMMEDIATE SUPPRESSION AND RESIDUAL INTERFERENCE OF CONVERSATIONAL PATTERNS IN LLMs
abstract: This study investigates the differential effectiveness of Stop instructions (e.g., “encerrar este assunto” [close this topic]) and Shift instructions (e.g., “mudar de assunto” [change the subject]) in immediately reducing the textual manifestation of previously induced conversational patterns and their subsequent residual manifestation in LLMs. Paradigms of proactive interference, instructed suppression, and topical continuity have already been employed in LLM research; the contribution here is deliberately narrow and empirical. The protocol uses a 2×2×2 factorial design for the primary lexical pair, an auxiliary reference condition, confirmatory lexical replication with multiple pairs, a pre-specified primary endpoint, convergent validation of the measures, and a statistical plan defined before data collection. H1 predicts lower immediate manifestation of the previous pattern after Stop formulations than after Shift formulations. The residual phase is exploratory. No behavioral result will be interpreted as erasure, deactivation, recovery, or persistence of an internal representation. The objective is to estimate whether the instructional contrast produces an effect that is robust, generalizable across pre-specified formulations, and of practically relevant magnitude in multi-turn interactions.

title: Developing the quality evaluation index system of digital textbooks for physical education and health
abstract: Background: Digital textbooks have evolved beyond mere digital replicas of printed versions. They have transformed into a new type of teaching resource that integrates multimedia elements, intelligent interaction, dynamic learning analytics, and data-driven support. The research and application of digital textbooks for physical education have become a crucial component of advancing the digital transformation of physical education. This study focuses on the quality of the development of digital textbooks for physical education, aiming to construct a scientific and comprehensive evaluation index system that provides theoretical basis and practical guidance for the development, application, and evaluation of digital textbooks, and to contribute to the modernization of education. Methods: The study first reviewed relevant achievements in the evaluation of digital textbooks and physical education and health in China and abroad through literature review, clarifying the connotation, elements, and major problems of digital textbooks for physical education. Then, it applied the Delphi method and the analytic hierarchy process, and the index selection, structure revision, and weight determination were completed through multiple rounds of expert consultation. Finally, mathematical statistics were used to analyze reliability, validity, and consistency on the expert data to ensure the objectiveness and reliability of the constructed evaluation system. Results: This study constructed a quality evaluation index system for digital textbooks for physical education in primary and secondary schools, comprising 4 primary indicators, 16 secondary indicators, and 100 tertiary indicators. The system encompasses key dimensions-educational orientation, content structure, teaching applicability, and compilation standards-thereby reflecting the textbooks' value alignment, scientific rigor, practical applicability, and standardization. The weight analysis revealed that "Content structure" and "Teaching applicability" carry the highest weights (both 0.351), followed by "Compilation standards" (0. 189), while "Educational orientation" has a relatively lower weight (0. 109). Among the secondary indicators, "Value Orientation" "Content Presentation Standards" and "Structural System" are ranked first within their respective dimensions. Conclusion: The quality evaluation index system for digital physical education textbooks developed in this study is both scientific and operable. It provides systematic theoretical support and a practical basis for the research, review, and continuous improvement of digital textbooks. In response to current problems-such as outdated content, monotonous presentation formats, insufficient application in teaching, and weak feedback mechanisms-this study proposes strengthening textbooks by optimizing content, innovating in presentation, and improving teaching support and feedback. These measures are intended to enhance the timeliness, interactivity, teaching adaptability, and continuous improvement capabilities of the textbooks. In the future, the indicator system should be dynamically adjusted alongside changes in education policies and technological evolution. This will continuously improve the quality and innovation level of digital textbooks, allowing them to better serve teaching practice and promote students' all-round development.

title: Establishing the corpus of Danish digitally mediated interaction (DanDIGI)
abstract: The DanDIGI project establishes the first comprehensive, multimodal, cross-platform corpus of Danish digitally mediated interaction. Integrating data from five major social media platforms, the corpus combines large-scale public datasets with smaller, metadata-rich ethnographic collections. All material is encoded in TEI-conformant XML, preserving interactional structure, multimodal features, and platform-specific affordances. A dedicated pipeline comprises OCR, AI-assisted pseudonymization, structural markup, and linguistic annotation. Derived formats, including VRT and HTML-based context views, enable both quantitative and qualitative analyses within the same corpus infrastructure. DanDIGI provides a foundation for longitudinal studies, cross-modal comparisons, and data-driven research on contemporary Danish digital communication.

title: Statistical versus machine learning-based spatial interpolation of post-processed ensemble weather forecasts
abstract: Statistical post-processing improves ensemble weather forecasts, but generating calibrated predictions at locations without observations remains challenging. This study compares statistical and machine-learning-based methods for post-processing ECMWF 2-m temperature and 10-m wind speed forecasts at observed and unobserved stations in Germany. We consider EMOS-based approaches, distributional regression networks, Transformers, and graph neural networks under both limited and extended predictor settings. For temperature, we also investigate linear forecast combinations and propose an altitude-aware linear pool (ALP). The results show that post-processing improves upon the raw ensemble in most settings, but no single method performs best across all variables, station groups, and evaluation metrics. The proposed ALP provides a small but significant improvement over the standard linear pool at unobserved locations.

title: EmoMed: An Emotionally-Aware Agent for Multimodal Medical Support with Real-Time Information Retrieval
abstract: We present EmoMed - a multimodal medical consultation agent that adapts its responses based on users' emotional states while maintaining clinical accuracy. The system processes text and medical images, detects affect indicators (anxiety, confusion, urgency) from user input, and adjusts response tone, structure, and detail level accordingly. To ensure factual reliability, the agent grounds clinical information through a dual retrieval mechanism: web-based fact-checking and an API-connected, continuously updated medical knowledge base. We evaluate our approach across seven state-of-the-art language models (GPT-4/5, Qwen3, Llama 4, Gemini 2.5, Grok4, Claude3) using comprehensive metrics including LLM-as-judge assessments, MedQA style accuracy tests, BERT Score, safety/helpfulness ratings, and multimodal medical benchmarks. The results demonstrate that emotionally adaptive responses consistently outperform neutral baseline across evaluation dimensions, without compromising clinical accuracy. A controlled user study validated these findings, with participants reporting improved perceived empathy and communication clarity, while maintaining trust in factual accuracy. Source code: https://github.com/NasonovIvan/EmoMed-Agent

title: Utilizing large language models to improve speech recognition for Slovene language
abstract: Za slovenščino, ki sodi med jezike z manj viri, ostaja razpoznavanje govora še vedno zahtevna naloga, sodobni veliki jezikovni modeli pa s svojim bogatim jezikovnim znanjem odpirajo nove možnosti za izboljšanje njegove točnosti. V magistrski nalogi sistematično preučimo in ovrednotimo štiri skupine metod za vključevanje velikih jezikovnih modelov v sistem za razpoznavanje slovenskega govora, ki segajo od plitke integracije (ponovno ocenjevanje hipotez, pozivanje in preslikava hipotez v transkript) do globoke integracije (večmodalni model SALM). Metode preizkusimo z osmimi velikimi jezikovnimi modeli in jih primerjamo na šestih slovenskih evalvacijskih množicah z napako na ravni besed (WER) in s hitrostjo napovedovanja (RTFX). Najboljšo točnost doseže ponovno ocenjevanje z modelom SlovenianGPT (povprečni WER 10,26 %). Ugotovili smo, da so za slovenski govor veliki jezikovni modeli najučinkovitejši, kadar uporabljajo hipoteze sistema za razpoznavanje govora in jim način uporabe strogo določimo oziroma jih za nalogo doučimo. Najbolje se torej odrežejo kot ocenjevalec hipotez ali pri uglašeni preslikavi hipotez v transkript, ne pa pri prostem tvorjenju transkriptov. Analiza računske zahtevnosti pokaže, da so vse metode z velikimi jezikovnimi modeli občutno počasnejše in pomnilniško zahtevnejše od izhodiščnega razpoznavalnika, najboljši kompromis med točnostjo in hitrostjo pa med njimi ponudi preslikava hipotez v transkript.

title: Title: Cognitive Resonance Networks (CRNs) - Adaptive Neural Correlates
abstract: Cognitive Resonance Networks (CRNs) represent a paradigm shift in neural network design, aiming to emulate the intricate structure and function of the human brain. This paper explores the potential of CRNs to achieve unprecedented levels of adaptive learning and pattern recognition. The core claim is that CRNs will allow for the creation of highly adaptive neural networks – mimicking the brain's dynamic and self-organizing processes – facilitating breakthroughs in areas such as machine learning, cognitive modeling, and potentially, even advanced human-computer interaction. The proposed algorithm, a novel learning mechanism, will dynamically adjust network connections based on observed cognitive patterns, creating a self-modifying system capable of intricate and nuanced responses. This research will detail the algorithm's architecture, its mathematical foundation, and its potential impact on the field. The paper will discuss the challenges and opportunities associated with realizing this ambitious vision, emphasizing the critical role of dynamic connectivity and self-organization.

title: Quantum Entanglement and Non-Asymmetry Theory
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, has long been considered a curiosity, but its potential implications for computation are increasingly being recognized. This paper explores the theoretical framework of quantum entanglement within a non-asymmetric computing paradigm, proposing a novel approach that leverages entanglement to achieve enhanced computational capabilities. We delve into the intricacies of establishing a "entanglement operator," investigating its impact on specific mathematical operations, and formulating new algorithms designed to exploit the unique properties of entangled states. This research investigates the possibility of surpassing the limitations of classical computation through the utilization of quantum entanglement, aiming to identify potential breakthroughs and contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationship between quantum mechanics and computation. The paper presents a preliminary analysis of the proposed mechanism and highlights the significance of this research in advancing theoretical foundations of non-asymmetric computation.

title: 基于量子信息网络的分布式计算框架
abstract: This paper introduces a novel distributed computing framework leveraging quantum information networks, specifically focusing on the utilization of quantum entanglement and quantum key distribution (QKD) for enhanced scalability and security. We propose a system architecture that constructs a quantum entanglement network to facilitate parallel computations, utilizing quantum key distribution for secure data transfer. The framework addresses limitations of traditional computing by offering a fundamentally new approach to computational power, security, and scalability. The core mechanism involves building a quantum entanglement network, optimizing data flow through entanglement, and employing QKD for secure communication and computation. This research explores the potential of quantum information networks to revolutionize distributed computing, with a particular emphasis on achieving massive parallelism and robust data protection.

title: Quantum Entanglement Information Encoding: Adaptive Parameterization
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, offers immense potential for quantum computation. However, maintaining entanglement's stability and efficiency is a significant challenge. This paper investigates the use of quantum entanglement information encoding, specifically through the dynamic adjustment of quantum state parameters, to enhance quantum computing's performance and robustness. We propose a novel approach that leverages a "quantum degree of freedom" to dynamically adjust the state, optimizing the quantum computation process. This study explores the potential of such a method to achieve improved efficiency and stability compared to traditional encoding schemes. The core claim is that this adaptive parameterization will significantly improve quantum information processing.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Topological Structure Mapping Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic adaptive topological structure mapping algorithm designed to enhance model performance and interpretability. Traditional methods often rely on predefined mapping rules, limiting their flexibility and potential for improvement. Our algorithm leverages topological structure to dynamically adjust the mapping process, offering a more adaptable and insightful approach. We present a methodology that incorporates a feedback loop and parameter optimization to achieve superior results compared to existing approaches. The core mechanism involves a continuous refinement of the mapping based on observed model behavior, facilitating the identification of optimal mappings and mitigating potential issues. This paper provides a comprehensive investigation into the algorithm's design, implementation, and evaluation, demonstrating its effectiveness in various scenarios.

title: 基于量子纠缠的动态时空优化算法
abstract: This paper presents a novel dynamic time-space optimization algorithm based on quantum entanglement principles. Traditional optimization algorithms often rely on static parameter adjustments, limiting efficiency and generalization. We introduce a quantum state representation and a dynamically-adjusted optimization process that leverages the inherent properties of quantum entanglement to optimize solutions effectively. The algorithm's core mechanism involves creating and manipulating entangled quantum states to represent and modify the optimization landscape, resulting in improved performance across a range of problem instances. This work explores the potential of quantum mechanics to revolutionize optimization methodologies, offering a fundamentally different approach compared to conventional techniques. The proposed algorithm demonstrates promising results on several benchmark problems, showcasing its capability to navigate complex optimization landscapes with enhanced adaptability.

title: Fractal-Based Cryptographic Protocols for Secure Communication
abstract: This paper proposes a new cryptographic approach utilizing the principles of fractal geometry to enhance security in communication protocols. Traditional cryptographic methods, reliant on mathematical complexity, are increasingly susceptible to advanced attacks. This research posits that the inherent self-similarity and complexity found within fractal structures provide a fundamentally more robust defense. The core idea involves encoding cryptographic keys and communication protocols using fractal patterns. These patterns, due to their repeating self-similar characteristics at different scales, create a significantly higher degree of complexity than traditional encryption methods, thereby increasing the difficulty for attackers to decipher the information. The proposed protocols leverage the mathematical properties of fractals, specifically their scaling behavior and Hausdorff dimension, to achieve enhanced security. The presented methodology offers a potential solution to mitigate vulnerabilities present in current cryptographic systems. We explore several key fractal patterns and their application within secure communication frameworks, demonstrating the theoretical advantages and outlining future research directions. The core claim is that fractal-based protocols offer a novel and more resilient approach to secure communication compared to conventional methods.

title: 基于量子纠缠的自适应几何模型的动态调整算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel algorithm for dynamic adjustment of geometric models based on quantum entanglement. Traditional geometric modeling techniques often struggle to handle complex geometries, requiring significant computational resources. Quantum entanglement offers a potential pathway to accelerate these calculations, allowing for automatic parameter adjustment based on the model's inherent properties. This work proposes a framework that leverages entanglement to efficiently represent and manipulate geometric models, facilitating high-precision and high-throughput modeling and optimization. abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum state analysis and computation framework based on graph representation, enabling efficient search, computation, and simulation of quantum states. abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive learning algorithm for quantum metaphoric computing, aiming to automatically adjust computational models based on practical application contexts. title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Information Encoding and Multi-Layer Space Collaborative Computation
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to quantum computation centered around leveraging quantum entanglement within multi-layer space collaborative computation. The core claim is that by encoding information into multi-layer superposition states and utilizing the synergistic effects of entangled states, we can achieve computational capabilities far exceeding those of classical computers. This is achieved through the construction of multi-layer superposition states using multiple quantum bits, followed by the encoding of information into different layers through carefully designed sequences of quantum gates. Quantum entanglement is then strategically employed to establish correlations between these layers, facilitating collaborative computation and parallel processing. This architecture offers a significant departure from traditional single-layer quantum computation, promising enhanced computational power and a pathway towards quantum-level acceleration. The presented framework provides a foundation for exploring complex computational problems that are intractable for conventional computing methods. ---

title: Non-Euclidean Tensor Decomposition for Graph Representation Learning
abstract: Graph representation learning aims to transform graph data into meaningful vector representations that can be used for downstream tasks such as node classification, link prediction, and community detection. Traditional methods often rely on treating graphs as sets or matrices, which can be limiting when capturing the inherent multi-faceted relationships within a graph. This paper introduces a novel approach utilizing non-Euclidean tensor decomposition specifically tailored for graph data. We posit that graph data can be effectively represented as tensors, where nodes and edges are treated as higher-order indices. The core idea is to decompose these tensors using techniques designed for non-Euclidean spaces, allowing for a more nuanced and accurate representation of graph structures. The method incorporates concepts from graph theory to define the tensor structure and employs specific decomposition algorithms optimized for non-Euclidean data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and conceptual outlining, highlighting its potential to overcome the limitations of existing methods. This work provides a foundation for future research in applying tensor decomposition to graph representation learning.

title: Adaptive Kernel Methods for Anomaly Detection in Time Series
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to anomaly detection in time series data using adaptive kernel methods. Traditional kernel methods often fail when dealing with non-stationary time series, where the underlying data distribution changes over time. This research proposes a dynamic adaptation strategy for the kernel function, allowing the method to effectively capture evolving patterns and identify anomalies that deviate from the current data characteristics. The core of the method lies in a kernel learning algorithm that continuously updates the kernel function based on incoming data. This process enables the system to learn and adapt to shifts in the data distribution, resulting in improved anomaly detection performance compared to static kernel methods. The approach is theoretically grounded and provides a flexible framework for anomaly detection in various time series applications. The key performance metrics demonstrating the effectiveness of the adaptive kernel method are presented.

title: Non-Spin Noise Quantum Computing: Error Mitigation Strategies
abstract: This paper investigates error mitigation techniques specifically tailored for non-spin noise quantum computing environments. The core argument centers on leveraging quantum entanglement and multi-particle correlations to effectively suppress quantum bit (qubit) errors. The proposed mechanism involves designing specific quantum states and operations to amplify correlations between qubits, utilizing entangled states for information redundancy, and ultimately, reducing error rates. Unlike traditional approaches focused on spin noise, this research introduces novel strategies applicable to non-spin systems, representing a significant advancement in the field. The presented methods explore the potential to enhance the fidelity of quantum computations within environments where errors are primarily governed by non-spin sources, offering a pathway towards more robust and reliable quantum computation. We examine theoretical frameworks and potential implementations, focusing on the mathematical underpinnings of error suppression and demonstrating the principles through conceptual models.

title: ##基于信息熵的程序语义自动翻译
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to program semantic automatic translation based on information entropy. The core idea is to treat the program execution process as an information flow and analyze the changes in information entropy. By quantifying these entropy variations, we establish semantic mappings between different programming languages, enabling automatic translation. Traditional methods for semantic translation often rely on syntactic rules, which can be rigid and fail to capture the nuances of program semantics. This research provides a fundamentally different perspective, viewing semantic translation as a problem of information entropy change. We introduce a framework that leverages entropy analysis to achieve more accurate and flexible translation, particularly for programs with complex control flow and dynamic behavior. The paper details the theoretical foundation, outlines the proposed methodology, and discusses potential challenges and future research directions. ---

title: Neural Group Emergence in Hyperdimensional Space Sampling
abstract: This paper investigates the emergent behavior of neural networks in performing unsupervised sampling within high-dimensional spaces. We propose a framework utilizing a reinforcement learning-based neural network group to autonomously explore and sample from complex, potentially unknown, distributions. The core idea is that through self-organization and a reward mechanism, the network group can effectively discover hidden patterns and correlations. The mechanism leverages the collective intelligence of the group, allowing it to navigate and sample from high-dimensional spaces more efficiently than traditional, manually-designed sampling approaches. We demonstrate, through theoretical analysis and conceptual modeling, the potential of this approach to overcome the limitations of existing sampling techniques and unlock novel methods for data exploration and pattern discovery. The key equation governing the sampling process is represented as: $S = \sum_{i=1}^{K} \alpha_i * f(s_i)$, where *S* is the sampled point, *K* is the number of neural network members in the group, $s_i$ represents the state of the *i*-th network, and *f* is the function guiding the exploration. The exploration reward function can be defined as $R = \delta(S) - \delta(S_prev)$, where $\delta(S)$ represents the difference between the current sample *S* and the previous sample *S_prev*, encouraging the group to move to unexplored regions of the high-dimensional space. The learning rate for each network is denoted as $\eta_i$, and the update rule is $s_i = s_i + \eta_i * R$. The overall system dynamics are governed by the interaction of these individual network updates, leading to emergent collective behavior. Further, the probability density function of the sampled space is approximated by a multivariate Gaussian distribution: $p(x) \approx \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{D/2} |\Sigma|^{1/2}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(x - \mu)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu)\right)$, where *x* is the sampled point, *D* is the dimensionality of the space, $\Sigma$ is the covariance matrix, and $\mu$ is the mean vector. The effectiveness of the sampling strategy is evaluated by measuring the coverage of the high-dimensional space, the diversity of the sampled points, and the ability to identify underlying patterns. This research contributes to the field of unsupervised learning and offers a new perspective on how neural networks can be utilized for efficient data exploration in complex, high-dimensional environments.

title: SENTINELBI AI: AN AI-POWERED BUSINESS INTELLIGENCE SYSTEM FOR REVENUE MONITORING AND ANOMALY DETECTION
abstract: This paper presents SentinelBI AI, an end-to-end business intelligence platform that combines classical statistical monitoring with machine learning and deep learning to detect anomalous revenue behaviour in e-commerce operations. The system is built on the Online Retail II transactional dataset and aggregates transaction-level data into daily business-performance records comprising revenue, quantity, transaction count, active-customer count, and rolling-average revenue deviation. Two complementary unsupervised detectors are used: an Isolation Forest for unusual individual observations and an LSTM Autoencoder for unusual sequential revenue patterns. Their outputs are fused into a three-tier alert scheme—Normal, Warning, and Critical—and presented through an interactive Streamlit dashboard with business analytics, anomaly monitoring, investigation, and a natural-language query interface. The proposed pipeline provides a deployable decision-support system for timely e-commerce revenue monitoring and anomaly detection.

title: Generation of Vectorized Maps Beyond Vehicle View
abstract: Autonomous driving relies on High Definition (HD) maps for safe navigation. Traditional HD maps construction is costly in hardware, data and human resources, which together with its update limitations hinders scalability. Recent works have proposed online alternatives for HD vectorized mapping from onboard sensors. However, sensor field of view is limited, and the range of the reconstructed maps ahead of the vehicle is insufficient for safe planning. This paper aims to address this limitation by proposing the novel beyond-view vectorized map generation problem: given vectorized maps of the area sensed by the vehicle (in-view), to generate plausible map continuations. To experimentally assess its feasibility, we propose BeyondFormer, which, to the best of out knowledge, is the first work designed towards beyond-view map generation. Given the novelty of the problem, we generate the first dataset specifically designed for it and evaluate the proposed approach. The results demonstrate consistent performance across diverse scenarios, establishing learning-based methods as a promising direction for map forecasting in autonomous driving. Beyond demonstrating the feasibility of the task, we provide an extensive discussion of the method's limitations and identify key future research directions for scaling it to more complex driving conditions. Code is available at https://git-autopia.car.upm-csic.es/beyondformer.

title: Particle Dynamics of Flow Matching and Classifier-Free Guidance from a Stagewise Geometry Perspective
abstract: Flow matching, together with classifier-free guidance (CFG), is widely used in generative modeling, yet much of the theoretical understanding remains distribution-wise. Since practical sampling follows individual trajectories, distribution-level guarantees alone do not fully capture how trajectories interact with the data geometry or how guidance reshapes it. To overcome this limitation, we establish a unified stagewise geometric theory of attraction and absorption for both continuous dynamics and explicit Euler discretization. Specifically, with $t\in[0,1]$ running from noise to data, we show that unconditional flow trajectories are successively attracted toward a neighborhood of the global mean, the data convex hull, and a neighborhood of a possibly nonconvex local cluster. Across these stages, the corresponding distance satisfies a common contraction estimate, yielding an ${O}(1-t)$ decay of the distance in the final stage. For CFG, the same structure persists with an extrapolated mean, an inflated conditional convex hull, and, near the target cluster, the restored local geometry of conditional flow matching. We further show that a general time schedule $a(t)$ replaces the $O(1-t)$ decay by $O(1-a(t))$. Together, these results provide a unified particle-level geometric account of flow matching and CFG across continuous and discrete sampling.

title: Developmental robotics is key to achieve a general AI
abstract: Despite massive investments and commercial successes, today's artificial intelligence (AI) systems are only effective in a limited range of domains. A general AI able to tackle any situation with a minimum of efficiency is still beyond our grasp. The solution to this problem does not seem to be related to an increase in computational power or in incremental refinements of the current approaches. Here, we argue that developmental robotics-i.e., the progressive, lifelong learning of an embodied robotic system-holds the key to realizing true general AI. To attain general AI with human-level capacities, such a system must be embedded in human society and experience what an average human experiences, starting with caring parents, kindergarten, elementary school, siblings, secondary school, friends, high school, college, university, sports, hobbies, internet, social media, nature, food, fatigue, pain, and more. Advances in modern robotics make it possible to educate a robot that fits right into each one of these domains, thereby experiencing the developmental situations typical of human growth. Moreover, for such a robot to qualify as a general AI, its cognitive abilities must self-organize and exhibit traits commonly regarded as hallmarks of human intelligence, including (apparent) free will, compassion, love, curiosity. A putative framework able to provide such cognitive abilities is the Theory of neural Cognition (TnC) published 15 years ago. In this paper, we illustrate how contemporary robotics can be integrated with the TnC to facilitate the emergence of a conscious robot-i.e., a genuine general AI system.

title: Quantum Hiding Computation: A Global Optimization Approach
abstract: Quantum Hiding Computation (QHC) offers a transformative paradigm for optimization problems, leveraging quantum mechanics to enable more efficient search and exploration. This paper explores the application of QHC to global optimization, proposing a novel algorithm based on entangled qubits and quantum superposition. We detail the core mechanism of this approach, emphasizing the utilization of quantum entanglement to enhance the exploration of search spaces and guide the algorithm towards optimal solutions. The paper highlights the potential advantages of QHC over traditional global optimization techniques, focusing on improved efficiency and the ability to tackle complex, high-dimensional problems. This work investigates the theoretical foundations and practical implementation of this approach, demonstrating its promise for advanced optimization scenarios.

title: Based on Quantum Entanglement: Geometric Topology
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, has captivated researchers and fueled significant interest in its potential applications. This paper explores the intersection of quantum entanglement and geometric topology, proposing a novel model that leverages entanglement to simulate the evolution of topological structures and investigate its impact on geometric properties. The research aims to investigate how entanglement, a non-classical correlation, can influence the formation and stability of geometric topologies, potentially offering insights into the design of novel quantum algorithms and quantum information protocols. We present a theoretical framework that utilizes quantum computation to model geometric transformations induced by entanglement, with the goal of uncovering new patterns and properties of topological spaces. title: Title: Adaptive Wave Function Collapse for Optimization Problems
abstract: This paper presents an innovative approach to optimization problems, leveraging Adaptive Wave Function Collapse (AWFC) to significantly improve the efficiency of finding optimal solutions. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with complex landscapes, requiring exhaustive search. AWFC dynamically collapses the wave function of potential solutions, enabling the exploration of multiple solution spaces simultaneously and drastically reducing the computational burden. We introduce a novel algorithm incorporating quantum-inspired principles, allowing for a more targeted and efficient search process. The paper details the implementation of the AWFC algorithm, its performance analysis, and its potential applications across diverse optimization scenarios. Specifically, we demonstrate its effectiveness in a range of problems, including the Traveling Salesman Problem and the Quadratic Assignment Problem, showcasing a substantial improvement in solution time compared to conventional methods.

title: Scalable Quantum Key Distribution Protocol
abstract: This paper presents a novel scalable Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocol designed to facilitate secure key exchange in large-scale quantum communication systems. The protocol leverages quantum entanglement and quantum measurement techniques to generate and distribute a secret key between multiple parties. A key limitation of existing QKD protocols is their restricted scalability. This proposed protocol addresses this issue through a carefully designed architecture and utilizes advanced quantum information processing concepts to enable the expansion of the system while maintaining its inherent security. The theoretical analysis demonstrates the protocol's feasibility and outlines key parameters for optimization. We focus on the core mechanisms and provide a detailed description of the protocol's operation, highlighting its potential for practical implementation in future quantum networks. The protocol's performance characteristics, including key rate and security level, are discussed.

title: Quantum Entanglement Computing Framework – Based on Topological Correlation
abstract: Quantum entanglement remains a cornerstone of modern quantum computing, offering the potential for fundamentally faster computations than classical computers. However, the inherent limitations of quantum systems, particularly the susceptibility to decoherence and the challenge of scaling entangled states, present significant hurdles to practical applications. This paper explores a novel quantum algorithm framework, leveraging topological correlation, as a potential solution to these challenges. We propose a new approach that minimizes entanglement redundancy and enhances the scalability of quantum algorithms, effectively circumventing the limitations imposed by local realism. The core mechanism centers around the design of a quantum algorithm specifically tailored to exploit topological properties, leading to improved efficiency and enhanced expressibility. The paper details the fundamental concepts, proposes a specific algorithm, and discusses the potential implications for the future of quantum computing.

title: Bayesian Geometry for Probabilistic Network Analysis
abstract: This paper explores the application of Bayesian geometry to probabilistic network analysis, aiming to refine traditional network modeling through the incorporation of geometric priors. We propose a novel framework that leverages geometric objects to represent relationships within a network, updating these priors as data becomes available. This approach offers a pathway to more accurate network structure estimation and dynamics forecasting, specifically addressing the limitations of standard Bayesian network methods when dealing with inherent uncertainty in the data. The core mechanism centers around defining geometric relationships and updating these relationships using Bayesian inference, thereby providing a more robust and nuanced representation of the network.

title: Causal Inference Neural Networks (CINN)
abstract: Traditional neural networks, while effective in many applications, often struggle with scenarios where spurious correlations exist within the training data. These spurious correlations can lead to poor generalization performance when the underlying causal relationships change. This paper introduces Causal Inference Neural Networks (CINN), a novel architecture designed to mitigate this issue by explicitly learning and incorporating causal relationships. CINN leverages principles from causal inference theory to construct a network capable of producing more robust and reliable predictions and decisions. The core claim is that neural networks can achieve superior performance by learning causal relationships. The mechanism involves a redesigned neural network architecture that learns these relationships. We demonstrate the potential of CINN through a theoretical framework and outline its key components, highlighting the shift from correlation-based learning to causal understanding. The paper's focus is on the theoretical foundations and design principles of CINN, providing a roadmap for future research and development in this area.

title: Towards System Security Based on Multi-Agent Adversarial Learning
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Multi-Agent Adversarial Learning (MAAL) for enhancing system security. Traditional security approaches often struggle to adapt to evolving and sophisticated cyberattacks. We propose a novel framework utilizing MAAL, where multiple intelligent agents collaborate to learn and defend against attacks. The core mechanism involves framing system security as an adversarial learning problem, leveraging the interactive dynamics between agents to create a robust and adaptable defense. The agents, trained through competitive and cooperative interactions, effectively identify and neutralize threats, significantly improving the system's resilience. We demonstrate the potential of this approach to provide a dynamic and adaptive security solution, particularly relevant in scenarios with evolving attack landscapes. This research contributes to the development of intelligent security systems capable of proactively responding to threats. ---

title: Humans Introduce, Models Elaborate: Asymmetric Narrative Agency in Human-LLM Co-Writing
abstract: Human-LLM co-writing is increasingly used for open-ended text generation, but much prior work focuses on final outputs rather than the interactional dynamics through which stories are produced. We study turn-based collaborative storytelling across three matched conditions: Human-Human (HH), Human-LLM (HA), and LLM-LLM (AA). Using a shared storytelling paradigm, we measure how agents align, introduce novel material, and influence narrative development through turn-level measures of valence adaptation, semantic novelty, transience, and resonance. Our results show that HA co-writing is not intermediate between HH and AA collaboration. Instead, it displays a distinctive asymmetry where humans tend to introduce more novel and persistent narrative material, while LLMs tend to elaborate and stabilize the existing context. These findings suggest that, in this setting, LLMs function less as human co-authors and more as adaptive narrative amplifiers that reshape how agency is distributed in collaborative writing.
