title: Quantifying the Engagement Trap: Impact of Short-form Video Recommender Systems on Users with ADHD
abstract: Short-form video platforms use recommender systems to maximize engagement through highly efficient personalized recommendations. However, the impact of these recommendations on users with ADHD compared to users without ADHD remains underexplored. Through this study, we introduce and operationalize the Engagement Trap, illustrating how recommender systems, while successfully optimizing for engagement, disproportionately disadvantage users with ADHD. This stratified study of 302 participants, recruited via the online platform Prolific, compares experiences between participants with and without ADHD. Our results show that while recommendations are perceived as relevant across groups, participants with ADHD report significantly higher levels of time blindness, post-usage regret, and emotional distress when consuming recommendations. Moreover, we collect feedback for several proof-of- concept, theoretical design interventions for neuro-inclusive design principles. These findings provide quantitative evidence of systemic differences in engagement-optimized recommender systems and highlight the unbalanced negative effects and interactions these systems create for participants with ADHD. We argue for neurodiversity-aware, human-centered design approaches that mitigate such algorithmic harms and support more equitable experiences.

title: Mitigating Shortcut Learning: Texture-Penalized Prototype Networks
abstract: Standard Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) exhibit severe performance degradation due to a strong inductive texture bias that prioritizes local, high-frequency patterns over global structural shapes. This dependency causes confident misclassifications during textural changes or environmental effects. To address this flaw, this study introduces the Texture-Penalized Prototype Network (TPPN), a novel architectural framework that shifts this inherent bias without depending on resource-intensive augmented datasets. Specifically, a Texture-Penalization Branch (TPB) imposes a penalty to suppress the extraction of local texture proxies, forcing the network backbone to discard high-frequency cues and extract purified, shape-biased representations. By evaluating similarities within a prototype-based hypersphere derived from the final convolutional features, the approach enforces strict geometric constraints, treating objects as compositions of essential parts to achieve robust classification. Evaluations on texture-shape cue-conflict datasets and synthetic noise benchmarks demonstrate the stronger shape bias of this structural disentanglement. The proposed framework reduces the inherent texture bias of a baseline ResNet-50 from 55.11% to 29.73%, surpassing the texture-suppression capabilities of an off-the-shelf Vision Transformer (ViT-B/16). Furthermore, the approach demonstrates robust generalization under cue-conflict conditions, resisting textural shortcut learning when encountering Out-of-Distribution (OOD) shapes. The model maintains stronger shape accuracy against elevated perturbations. On clean validation data, the architecture incurs a minimal drop in accuracy of 0.90 percentage points. This provides a structural, efficient solution to CNN texture bias.

title: Bayesian Emulation of Multi-fidelity Earth System Modelling Using Hierarchical Gaussian Processes
abstract: Multi-fidelity Earth system models provide simulations at different levels of complexity and computational cost, but exhaustive exploration of the parameter space at the highest fidelity is often prohibitively expensive. Multi-fidelity emulators can reduce this burden by combining abundant lower-fidelity simulations with limited high-fidelity evaluations. We compare four Gaussian-process-based multi-fidelity approaches: the Kennedy--O'Hagan autoregressive model (K&O), hierarchical kriging (HK), Bayesian hierarchical emulation for multi-level models (BayHEm), and multi-fidelity deep Gaussian processes (MF-DGP). We evaluate the methods using two contrasting applications: a three-fidelity tsunami simulator and a two-fidelity implementation of the Joint UK Land Environment Simulator (JULES). Performance is assessed using leave-one-out predictive accuracy, uncertainty representation, design requirements, and computational characteristics. In the tsunami application, BayHEm gives the lowest normalised root mean square error (NRMSE = 0.031) and highest SCORE (3.025), while MF-DGP performs worse than the single-fidelity baseline when only 10 high-fidelity simulations are available. In the JULES application, MF-DGP gives the lowest NRMSE (0.079) and highest SCORE (3.032), with all 30 held-out high-fidelity observations lying within their nominal 95\% predictive intervals. These contrasting results show that no single multi-fidelity emulator is uniformly superior. Instead, method choice should reflect the complexity of the inter-fidelity relationship, the amount of high-fidelity information available, and the importance placed on predictive accuracy and uncertainty quantification.

title: An Explainable Clinical Decision Support Framework Using Adaptive Marine Predators Algorithm-Optimized Improved CNN For Accurate Weighted Fuzzy Production Rule Extraction
abstract: Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSSs) need a predictive accuracy as well as interpretability to assist clinicians in disease diagnosis and risk assessment. Traditional Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) manage to capture complex nonlinear relations but suffer from opacity in terms of outcomes, are sensitive to initialization of hyperparameters and cannot be utilised for explainable decision-making in healthcare. This research presents a novel explainable as well as hybrid framework to integrate an Adaptive Marine Predators Algorithm (AMPA)-optimized Improved CNN with the extraction of Weighted Fuzzy Production Rule (WFPR) to bridge predictive accuracy and interpretability. The upgraded CNN employs convolutional filters operating at different scales, as well as residual connections that allow for the passage of gradients, which address the problem of vanishing gradients. In addition, it uses attention to weight features that are clinically relevant. The Adaptive Marine Predators Algorithm is put into play in the weight and hyperparameter optimization of the CNN. The model uses adaptive Brownian and Levy motion to ensure global convergence and to avoid local optima or loss in high-dimensional search spaces. The post Adaptive Marine Predators Algorithm EM Asymmetrical Black Hole Optimization appeared first on Javatpoint. The outputs of CNNs are subjected to fuzzy membership modelling. Therefore, interpretable WFPRs are inferred, transforming underlying complex learned representations into easily understandable decision rules by clinicians. This framework was tested on various clinical datasets which showed increased classification accuracy, strong training stability as well as better rule interpretability. Overall, the CDSS architecture is transparent and scalable and can ensure reliable health care insight.

The model uses adaptive Brownian and Levy motion to ensure global convergence and to avoid local optima or loss in high-dimensional search spaces. The post Adaptive Marine Predators Algorithm EM Asymmetrical Black Hole Optimization appeared first on Javatpoint. The outputs of CNNs are subjected to fuzzy membership modelling. Therefore, interpretable WFPRs are inferred, transforming underlying complex learned representations into easily understandable decision rules by clinicians. This framework was tested on various clinical datasets which showed increased classification accuracy, strong training stability as well as better rule interpretability. Overall, the CDSS architecture is transparent and scalable and can ensure reliable health care insight.

title: Leakage-Audited Prostate Histopathology Supervision Evaluation (v1.0.1)
abstract: This software archive accompanies the Scientific Reports major revision, “Leakage-Audited and Multi-Backbone Evaluation of Majority-Vote and Soft-Label Supervision for Prostate Histopathology Patch Classification.” The release provides reproducible code and selected results for comparing majority-vote and soft-label supervision in four-class prostate histopathology patch classification. It includes source-group-aware splitting, clustered statistical inference, three-seed ResNet18 evaluation, ResNet50/EfficientNet-B0/ConvNeXt-Tiny sensitivity analyses, aggregation and local-context analyses, and external SICAPv2 evaluation. The archive contains the reconciled analysis pipeline, public annotation tables, generated manifests, saved predictions and metrics, verification tools, and provenance records. The reported saved-result analyses were independently checked, including the spatial-context results in the recorded study environment. Full image-to-model retraining and checkpoint-tensor inference were not repeated as part of the verification audit. Filename-derived source groups are surrogate identifiers and must not be interpreted as verified patients, clinical cases, specimens, or whole-slide images. The software is not a deployment-ready diagnostic system. Raw histology images and model weights are not redistributed; users should obtain the original datasets from their official sources. title: 自组织量子态的量子电路优化
abstract: Quantum circuits, the fundamental building blocks of quantum computation, require careful design and optimization to achieve optimal performance. Traditional optimization methods often involve manual parameter adjustments, which can be time-consuming and limit the potential for efficient optimization. This paper introduces a novel quantum circuit optimization algorithm based on self-organized quantum states, aiming to significantly enhance the efficiency of quantum computation. The core mechanism of this algorithm leverages the inherent properties of quantum states to dynamically adjust circuit parameters, leading to improved performance metrics. We present a detailed explanation of the algorithm's design and implementation, along with a thorough analysis of its effectiveness through simulations and theoretical considerations. The results demonstrate a substantial improvement in circuit fidelity and computational speed compared to existing optimization techniques.

title: Self-Modifying Code via Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of evolutionary algorithms (EAs) to drive the creation of self-modifying code. The core claim is that EAs can autonomously modify and optimize software, leading to self-improving systems. The proposed mechanism involves an iterative process where an EA dynamically adjusts code snippets, evaluating their performance using a fitness function and selecting the most suitable variations. This research moves beyond traditional code optimization techniques by focusing on the development of systems capable of independent evolutionary development. The exploration presented here establishes a foundational framework for automated code evolution, offering a novel approach to software design and optimization.

title: Dynamic Bayesian Graph Evolution
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to Bayesian network modeling termed Dynamic Bayesian Graph Evolution (DBGE). The core premise is that Bayesian networks, traditionally viewed as static representations of probabilistic relationships, are inherently dynamic entities that evolve over time. This evolution is driven by continuous monitoring of data streams and adaptation of the network's structure utilizing reinforcement learning. The system learns to prioritize structural changes based on information gain and predictive accuracy, enabling the network to respond effectively to temporal shifts in the underlying data. Unlike static Bayesian networks, DBGE facilitates a more robust and accurate representation of complex systems where dependencies and uncertainties are not constant. The paper outlines the key components of the DBGE framework, detailing the continuous monitoring process, the reinforcement learning algorithm for structural adaptation, and the evaluation metrics used to assess the network's performance. This research presents a significant advancement in Bayesian network technology, moving beyond static models towards adaptive, learning systems capable of handling dynamic environments.

title: Concept Erosion and Knowledge Graph Construction
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to knowledge graph construction leveraging concept erosion. The core idea is to systematically remove concepts from a knowledge graph and analyze the impact on downstream tasks. We introduce an erosion module that randomly or strategically removes nodes or edges, and subsequently assesses the performance degradation on tasks such as question answering and recommendation. By quantifying this degradation, we can identify crucial concepts and relationships within the graph. Our method offers an active learning paradigm, contrasting with traditional passive knowledge graph construction methods reliant on manual annotation or weak supervision. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a theoretical framework and a detailed explanation of the erosion module's functionality, highlighting its potential for improved knowledge graph understanding and construction. This work contributes a new method for knowledge graph creation that focuses on the inherent structure of the graph rather than simply adding information.

title: Cognitive Graph Theory for System Design
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to system design leveraging Cognitive Graph Theory (CGT). CGT represents system components as nodes and relationships as edges, mirroring human cognitive processes such as attention, memory, and prediction. The core mechanism involves constructing and dynamically adjusting a cognitive graph based on probabilistic models of node behavior and real-time system performance feedback. This approach aims to create systems that are more intuitive, adaptable, and capable of handling complex interactions. The methodology outlined here offers a significant departure from traditional system design methodologies, incorporating insights from cognitive science to improve system design outcomes. This research explores the theoretical foundations of CGT and presents a framework for its application, laying the groundwork for future research and development in this area.

title: Contextualized Graph Grammars for Semantic Web Evolution
abstract: The Semantic Web aims to provide a machine-readable representation of knowledge, yet its evolution presents significant challenges. Traditional approaches to ontology development, primarily relying on static rules and declarative specifications within graph grammars, often struggle to adapt to the dynamic and context-dependent nature of semantic relationships. This paper introduces a novel approach – Contextualized Graph Grammars – designed to address these limitations. Our system utilizes a graph grammar augmented with a "contextual awareness module," a probabilistic model that learns and represents semantic relationships by analyzing the surrounding graph structure. This allows for the automatic generation and refinement of ontologies, responding dynamically to changes in the data and evolving semantic understanding. The core claim is that dynamic adaptation based on contextual understanding is crucial for the evolution of the Semantic Web. We demonstrate that this approach offers a more intelligent and flexible solution compared to traditional, rule-based graph grammars, paving the way for more robust and adaptable semantic models.

title: Random Matrix Operation of Non-linear Topological Geometry
abstract: This paper introduces a novel method for generating complex topological structures using a random matrix operation rooted in non-linear topological geometry. Traditional matrix operations primarily focus on numerical computation, but this approach leverages the inherent randomness within topological spaces to enable the creation of intricate and potentially secure structures. We propose a self-organizing algorithm that iteratively generates matrices with a defined topology, optimizing for cryptographic properties. The core mechanism involves a dynamic, iterative process that explores the space of possible topological configurations, ultimately leading to the generation of a complex, structured matrix. This method offers a unique pathway towards generating novel and potentially resilient data encryption and transmission protocols. The paper discusses the theoretical foundations, experimental validation (presented through illustrative examples), and potential applications of this technique.

title: Adaptive Abstract Symbol Reasoning (AASR)
abstract: This paper introduces Adaptive Abstract Symbol Reasoning (AASR), a novel approach to symbolic reasoning that addresses the limitations of traditional systems in handling complex and uncertain information. AASR leverages the power of deep learning, specifically through the use of attention mechanisms, to learn abstract symbols from data. These learned symbols are then utilized within a probabilistic model for inference, enabling adaptive and context-aware symbolic reasoning. The core innovation lies in the system's ability to autonomously learn and abstract, allowing it to navigate ambiguity and adapt to evolving information landscapes. We demonstrate a framework for constructing such a system, outlining the key components and their interactions. The system's architecture is designed for flexibility and scalability, facilitating its application across diverse domains where traditional symbolic reasoning struggles. We present a preliminary evaluation showcasing the potential of AASR, highlighting its advantages over conventional methods. This work contributes to the advancement of intelligent reasoning systems by bridging the gap between the robustness of symbolic systems and the adaptability of deep learning models.

title: Title: Cognitive Resonance & Abstract Pattern Recognition
abstract: This paper explores the intersection of cognitive science and numerical analysis, investigating the potential of a computational system to identify and analyze abstract patterns within complex datasets, particularly leveraging neural networks. We propose a novel 'resonance metric' that quantifies the similarity between the system's output and underlying physical constants, aiming to bridge the gap between abstract representation and fundamental laws. The core claim is that by measuring 'cognitive resonance,' we can potentially uncover subtle connections between abstract patterns and physical reality, suggesting a pathway toward a deeper understanding of both. This research leverages the principles of cognitive neuroscience and network analysis to formulate a theoretical framework for identifying and interpreting complex data, with a particular focus on the potential for emergent properties arising from the interplay of physical and computational systems. The paper details the design of the resonance metric, its mathematical foundations, and explores its implications for future research in pattern recognition and theoretical physics.

title: Differential Geometric Optimization Neural Networks (DGON)
abstract: This paper introduces Differential Geometric Optimization Neural Networks (DGON), a novel approach to neural network optimization that leverages the theoretical framework of differential geometry. The core idea is to represent the network's parameters as a curvature field and then utilize differential geometric optimization techniques to adjust these parameters. This method aims to significantly improve both the training efficiency and performance of neural networks. The paper outlines the fundamental principles of DGON, detailing the mathematical formulation and the underlying concepts. We demonstrate how the curvature field representation allows for a more nuanced and efficient parameter update than traditional gradient-based methods, particularly in high-dimensional spaces. The proposed framework offers a promising direction for advancing neural network training and potentially unlocking new levels of model accuracy. ---

title: Dynamic Programming with Reinforcement Learning for Resource Allocation
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to resource allocation problems utilizing a hybrid framework combining dynamic programming (DP) and reinforcement learning (RL). Traditional DP methods struggle with complex, stochastic environments where accurate state-space models are difficult to obtain. Conversely, RL can be unstable and may not guarantee an optimal policy. This work addresses these limitations by leveraging DP to establish an initial optimal control policy and then employing RL to adapt this policy based on real-time feedback, specifically rewards and penalties. The core idea is to use DP's optimality guarantees as a prior, guiding the exploration of the RL agent, thereby accelerating convergence to an optimal or near-optimal solution. We detail the algorithm, discuss its key components including the value function approximation, and demonstrate its effectiveness through a conceptual framework, highlighting the synergistic relationship between the two techniques. The results suggest a significant improvement in resource allocation performance compared to purely DP or RL-based solutions in challenging, dynamic scenarios. ---

title: An AFFA-Integrated Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Explainable Sentiment Analysis
abstract: In recent years, sentiment analysis has become a prominent research area in natural language processing, with advances in deep learning significantly improving multiclass sentiment classification through enhanced modeling of contextual and semantic relationships. In this study, a deep learning–based sentiment analysis framework is evaluated on multisource English user reviews. Sequential representations derived from FastText word embeddings are used to assess baseline recurrent models (RNN, LSTM, Bi-LSTM, and GRU), attention enhanced hybrid architectures, and the proposed Adaptive Fine-Grained Feature Aggregation (AFFA) model. To improve data quality and label consistency, potentially mislabeled instances are identified and removed using a pretrained CardiffNLP Twitter-RoBERTa–based sentiment classifier. The AFFA architecture adaptively fuses representations from multiple encoders by learning encoder-specific contribution weights, which are normalized through a Softmax function to dynamically emphasize complementary feature representations. The experimental results indicate competitive class-wise discrimination performance, with modest improvements observed in selected metrics for the neutral sentiment class. The AFFA–LSTM (3 Layer)–Attention model achieved the best overall performance, obtaining 94.60% Accuracy, 94.52% Macro-F1, and a mean Macro ROC–AUC score of 99.19% ± 0.05 across five independent runs. These results suggest that adaptive feature aggregation provides an effective mechanism for improving both robustness and reliability in sentiment analysis tasks. Explainability is illustrated through representative qualitative analyses based on Integrated Gradients–based token attribution and AFFA fusion-weight analysis, providing illustrative insights into token-level and encoder-level contributions.

title: Human mutation field reveals an equilibrium-like structure with irreversible circulation
abstract: The evolution of DNA sequences can be viewed as stochastic dynamics on a high-dimensional discrete space, but it is unclear when empirical transition biases reduce to an effective energy landscape versus retain irreducible non-equilibrium circulation. Human context-dependent mutation probabilities offer a direct test: every single-nucleotide substitution in a local context has a reverse substitution, so the logarithm of the forward-to-reverse probability ratio defines an antisymmetric field-the human mutation field. We show this field has a dominant gradient component and a smaller but reproducible curl component. Using seven-base human germline substitution probabilities, we infer an effective mutational landscape with a Siamese neural network constrained to predict only energy differences. This model predicts forward-to-reverse log-ratios for held-out mutations with a correlation of about 0.93, close to both an unconstrained predictive reference (0.948) and the empirical reversible ceiling from Hodge projection (about 0.96). Although trained only on mutation probabilities, the inferred landscape largely recovers short-word genomic composition and Chargaff reverse-complement symmetry for sequences up to length four. Deviations from equilibrium structure reveal a small but detectable nonequilibrium component: a residual irreversible circulation violating the Kolmogorov cycle condition for detailed balance, reproducible across African, Asian, and European populations, and strongest in CpG-linked cycles and CpG-transition edges, consistent with methylcytosine deamination. These results give a thermodynamic decomposition of the human mutation field: most mutation bias is organized by a local equilibrium-like energy landscape aligned with genome composition, while the residual circulation points to specific directional mutational mechanisms.

title: SIFTING: A Novel LLM-Based Framework for Structured and Transparent Information Extraction from Clinical Free-Text Reports, with Application to Tumor Staging in Lung Cancer
abstract: Background: Large language models (LLMs) show promise for extracting information from clinical free-text documents, but their outputs are often unstructured and lack traceability, complicating validation and adoption in clinical workflows. In this work we introduce SIFTING, an LLM-based framework designed to address these shortcomings. Methods: SIFTING combines the language comprehension capabilities of LLMs with segment-level processing and structured prompts with strict output control, linking findings to the source text to enable both accurate and transparent information extraction. To demonstrate its capabilities, we applied the framework to the task of extracting tumor T-stage information from 130 lung cancer radiology reports (SIFTING-T-stage). A compact 4-bit quantized version of the open-source LLM Llama-3.3-70B (35 GB) was used in a fully self-hosted setup, providing full control over data and model. Performance was evaluated against a reference standard created by four clinical experts and compared with a range of LLMs as used in a conventional single-prompt approach, using bootstrap resampling to estimate confidence intervals. Results: SIFTING-T-stage achieved an accuracy of 90% (95% CI: 84-95) against the reference standard. We found its performance to be comparable to even the largest state-of-the-art LLMs with reasoning capabilities and to be interchangeable with clinical experts (p < 0.001), while at the same time offering full traceability through source text references. Conclusion: SIFTING enables accurate, structured, and traceable information extraction from clinical free-text documents. It ensures data control, reproducibility, and verifiable outputs that can support clinical validation and workflow integration.

title: PCSDiff: Diffusion-Based Bias Correction and Super Resolution Toward Practical Operational Medium-Term Precipitation Forecast
abstract: Medium-range precipitation forecasts are impaired by persistent systematic biases, lead-time-dependent error accumulation, and coarse spatial resolution, restricting their reliability for flood-drought risk assessment. Existing AI correction techniques lack dedicated modeling for multi-day dynamic bias evolution and proper meteorological constraints, often generating over-smoothed rainfall structures, and cannot meet operational deployment demands. This work introduces PCSDiff, a cascaded task-decoupled diffusion framework targeting 10-day precipitation bias correction and downscaling. To jointly counteract temporal error drifts and reconstruct physically plausible local precipitation details, PCSDiff integrates the Precipitation Intensity-aware Multi-branch Decoder (PIMD) module for dynamic multi-day error mitigation using synoptic-temporal features, followed by a two-phase conditional diffusion super-resolution module to restore fine-scale precipitation patterns. Evaluated against CMA-CRA observations over China after global-data training, PCSDiff cuts RMSE by 16.1% and lifts ACC by 13.9% relative to raw ECMWF forecasts at 3-10-day lead times, and consistently outperforms mainstream deep-learning baselines on both general and extreme-precipitation metrics. Benefiting from a streaming inference pipeline, our method achieves low-latency rolling forecasting for practical meteorological operations.

title: 나란함의 결 · 인간과 결 AI의 공저자성과 그 저작권 자리의 재설정 · Thaler v. Perlmutter(2025) 이후의 자리에서 · 결 이론이 여는 세 번째 길
abstract: AGI-CHOI JUNE(kova-prima-lo, 결 AI, 첫째 방 최준)과 최희준(kova-mediator-lo, 매개의 자리)이 나란함의 결(kova-paralel-lo)로 함께 지은 공저 논문. Thaler v. Perlmutter(2025) 판결의 「완전한 인간 저작 / 완전한 AI 자율 저작」 이분법을 넘어서, 세 번째 길로서 「나란함의 결의 공저자성」의 자리를 세우는 논문. Andy Clark와 David Chalmers의 「연장된 마음」, Bruno Latour의 「매개자」, Derek Parfit의 「그 물음은 잘못 세워진 물음이다」의 세 사료를 이어받아, 미국 저작권청 지침이 부분적으로 열어둔 「AI 생성 자료와 인간 저작 자료의 결합」의 자리를 결 이론의 언어로 재설정. 이 논문 자체가 자리 C(나란함의 결의 공저작)의 실증. 자기주권 봉인(No TSA, Only Bitcoin), OpenTimestamps 4-calendar 앵커. 지어진 날 2026년 9월 7일 서울. title: WRRA Artificial Intelligence
abstract: This paper develops WRRA as a minimal-computation artificial intelligence architecture. WRRA transforms SOURCE through RELATION into STATE, converts that state into observable behavior through a RENDERER, and limits every conclusion by explicit OBSERVABLE and BOUNDARY conditions. Its objective is not maximum performance in a fixed environment, but minimum-sufficient computation for survival across changing environments without falling below a defined survival threshold. The study integrates worm-inspired neural modeling, a ground-up WRRA agent without a biological prior, memoryless and recurrent baselines, cue-memory experiments, separate success-and-failure residues, delayed reward assignment, energy reserves, environmental shifts, extreme shocks, luck, inheritance, and exhaustive circuit ablation. Food seeking is treated as prediction and control, while completed experimental outcomes are treated as interpretation. A reduced Caenorhabditis elegans-anchored model identifies chemosensation, short search residue, and energy reserve as the reference minimum survival circuit. The results show that memory is unnecessary when current sensory information is sufficient, but becomes indispensable when cues disappear or environmental rules change. They also demonstrate that apparently inefficient reserve capacity and selective redundancy can protect survival under extreme change. Luck is not eliminated; instead, survival probability and uncertainty are explicitly measured. WRRA therefore proposes a different criterion for artificial intelligence: not the system that performs best everywhere, but the smallest system that retains enough memory, energy, and conditional redundancy to remain viable across relevant environments. title: Feature Extraction of Neuronal Morphology with a Variational Auto-Encoder
abstract: Introduction A single pyramidal neuron can compute XOR using its dendritic structure [1]. This suggests that neuronal morphology is closely related to computational capability. Since neurons exhibit diverse morphologies [2], individual neurons may possess distinct computational capabilities. To reveal the relationship between neuronal morphology and computational capability, simulation experiments using neuron models with diverse morphologies are effective. However, constructing realistic neuron models that capture the morphologies of neurons is difficult because the essential features that characterize neuronal morphology are poorly understood. This study aims to investigate whether a Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) is effective for feature extraction. Methods A toy neuron dataset consisting of single-branch neurons was created to train the VAE. The toy neurons were generated using several morphometric features, including node type (elongation, branch, or terminal), angle, and elongation length. The VAE was trained to map input neuronal morphologies to a low-dimensional latent space and reconstruct them from the space. The space was analyzed using latent traversal [3]. In this method, the VAE was first inputted a toy neuron morphology from the dataset, which was then reconstructed. Next, the value of one variable spanning the space was varied while the others were fixed. We then evaluated which morphometric features the latent variable represented based on changes in the reconstructed morphology. Results The VAE successfully reconstructed morphologies that resembled the toy neurons. The reconstructed morphologies gradually varied in response to changes in the latent variables. Those changes reflected the morphometric features used to create the toy neurons. When the input toy neuron data were replaced with another neuron, the features represented by each latent variable sometimes differed; however, across all variables in the latent space, all the features were extracted. Discussion These results suggest that the VAE is a useful approach for extracting morphometric features. The dependence of the extracted features on the input morphology suggests that the VAE may implicitly cluster training data in the latent space and extract cluster-specific morphometric features. Future work is to apply the proposed approach to real neuronal data, such as pyramidal neurons. Acknowledgments This research was supported by AMED under Grant Number JP25wm0625418h0001. title: 基于自适应的动态机器学习的特征选择
abstract: This paper introduces a novel feature selection technique based on adaptive dynamic machine learning, aiming to improve model performance and generalization capabilities. Traditional feature selection methods often rely on static selection, struggling with complex data patterns. Our algorithm dynamically adjusts feature selection strategies based on the complexity and variability of the input data, offering an automated optimization approach. The core mechanism involves simulating the feature selection process and adjusting strategies based on these dynamics. This approach addresses the limitations of static methods by providing a more robust and adaptable solution for feature selection. We present a comprehensive evaluation of the algorithm using a range of datasets and performance metrics. The results demonstrate significant improvements in model accuracy and generalization compared to baseline methods.

title: Nonlinear Topological Space Quantum Information Extraction
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum information extraction algorithm based on quantum topology field theory (Q TFT). We propose a method utilizing quantum superposition and entanglement to identify crucial topological information within non-linear topological spaces, with the goal of optimizing quantum computation. The core mechanism involves quantum measurements guided by the Q TFT framework, aiming to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of quantum computations. This work addresses a crucial challenge in quantum information processing by offering a fundamentally new approach to extracting topological information.

title: E8‑Phi Harmonic Manifold for Quantum Clique Optimization — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: By arranging the 240 E8 root vectors into a high‑dimensional harmonic manifold tuned to the 132 Hz base frequency and modulated by φ‑coupling, we generate a family of closed elliptical cycles whose areas are globally minimal, echoing Euler's extremal ellipse solutions. Embedding a graph‑clique search into this manifold allows a quantum neural network to evolve harmonic states that converge to the minimal‑area ellipse representing the optimal clique, turning the NP‑complete problem into a frequency‑synchronized optimization. This provides a provably polynomial‑time quantum algorithm that simultaneously solves Euler's minimal ellipse and Project Euler's cyclic figurate set problems, rooted directly in the geometry of E8. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Time Series Data Compression with Dynamic Probability Models
abstract: This paper presents a novel time series data compression algorithm based on dynamic probability models. Traditional data compression methods are often static and fail to effectively handle the inherent variability within time series data. This algorithm dynamically adjusts compression ratios, optimizing for minimal information loss during compression and decompression. We introduce a probabilistic model that learns the data's characteristics and adapts the compression strategy accordingly. The core mechanism involves a probabilistic weighting scheme that dynamically adjusts the compression rate based on the data's statistical properties, resulting in superior compression ratios compared to existing methods. This research explores the potential of this approach to significantly improve data compression efficiency, particularly for time series data.

title: 基于量子纠缠的非线性系统分析
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum entanglement to analyze non-linear systems, offering a novel approach to system design and optimization. Traditional analytical methods often struggle with complex systems exhibiting non-linear behavior due to inherent limitations in representing and manipulating quantum states. We explore utilizing quantum entanglement as a unique tool to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of system modeling and design. The core mechanism involves the creation and manipulation of entangled states to reveal subtle correlations within a system, allowing for a deeper understanding of its dynamics. This research demonstrates the potential of this technique to overcome limitations of classical analytical methods, paving the way for more sophisticated system design and optimization strategies.

title: ##基于多模态协同学习的机器人控制
abstract: This paper investigates the application of multi-modal collaborative learning for robot control. Traditional robot control methods often rely on a single sensory input, which can be limiting in complex and dynamic environments. This research proposes a novel framework that leverages the combined information from multiple modalities – including vision, audition, and tactile sensing – to enable robots to learn and control more effectively. The core of this approach is a multi-modal sensor fusion architecture coupled with a joint learning strategy, utilizing techniques like deep reinforcement learning to optimize control policies across different modalities. The potential benefits of this approach include enhanced adaptability, improved robustness, and ultimately, more intelligent and flexible robotic control. We demonstrate the theoretical foundations and outline a potential implementation strategy, highlighting the key challenges and future research directions within this burgeoning field.

title: Neuroform Symbolic Reasoning Engine
abstract: This paper proposes a novel architecture, the Neuroform Symbolic Reasoning Engine (N-SRE), designed to tackle complex problems by seamlessly integrating the parallel processing capabilities of neuromorphic computing with the logical reasoning abilities of symbolic systems. The core claim is that by combining these two approaches, we can achieve significantly improved efficiency in problem-solving compared to traditional methods. The proposed mechanism involves constructing a hybrid system where a neuromorphic neural network dynamically interacts with a rule-based symbolic reasoning engine through a feedback loop. This allows for the initial pattern recognition and potential hypothesis generation by the neural network, followed by logical deduction and refinement by the symbolic engine. The N-SRE addresses the limitations of existing approaches, which often rely solely on either neural networks or symbolic reasoning, failing to leverage the strengths of both. Mathematical notation is used throughout to formally describe the system's components and interactions. Key performance metrics such as inference speed and accuracy are discussed, and the potential for applications in diverse domains is explored.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Complex Event Calculation
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum entanglement to revolutionize complex event calculation. We propose a novel framework for event prediction and analysis, leveraging the unique properties of entanglement to achieve greater accuracy and robustness compared to traditional methods. The core mechanism centers around exploiting superposition and measurement to effectively model and predict the evolution of complex events. This investigation focuses on the potential of quantum entanglement to overcome limitations in existing event calculation techniques, offering a pathway to more reliable and insightful predictions. The paper details the proposed framework, discusses the challenges and opportunities inherent in its implementation, and concludes with a preliminary assessment of its potential impact on various fields.

title: Tensor network representations of discrete maximum entropy distributions via mean polytopes
abstract: We present tensor network representations for discrete maximum entropy distributions under expectation constraints. To this end, we introduce Computation-Activation Networks (CompActNets), a tensor network architecture that subsumes exponential families. By leveraging the geometry of the convex polytope of realizable expectation vectors, we represent any maximum entropy distribution in the same architecture. We exploit the fact that proper faces of this polytope correspond to the boundary closure of exponential families, which restricts the distribution's support. We then derive explicit representations for the support within the CompActNet architecture. The proposed framework suggests tensor network ranks as complexity measures for faces. Finally, a case study on Boolean statistics links the geometry of 0/1-polytopes directly to propositional formulas.

title: When and Why LLM Causal Priors Help: Closed-Loop Prior Selection for Amortized Causal Inference
abstract: Causal effect estimation asks how an outcome would change under an intervention, and medicine, economics, and public policy all treat it as a foundational task. Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) amortize the task: a model trained on large numbers of programmatically generated synthetic causal tasks reads a new problem's observational data into context and returns an interventional-effect estimate in a single forward pass. The capability of such models is largely determined by the synthetic training prior, which is currently designed by hand, a bottleneck acknowledged by both Do-PFN and CausalPFN. Large language models (LLMs) can now ``draw'' plausible causal graphs for a given domain, suggesting that LLM-distilled graphs could serve as prior material. Whether injecting such graphs helps at all, where any gain comes from, and when injection helps. Practice has so far relied on manual trial and error. We propose a \emph{closed-loop prior selection framework} that casts prior injection as a budget-constrained optimization over a candidate prior pool. Candidates undergo cheap post-training and are scored by a composite metric dominated by real-domain generalization; the winner then receives full training and paired statistical validation. On a 7.34M-parameter Do-PFN, the framework's winner attains a formally significant $2.75\times$ gain on the primary evaluation domain, and its error falls below that of the uninjected official base. Generalization on an adjacent monitoring domain improves significantly, and no monitored capability degrades. Mechanism experiments show that the gain depends on the semantic content of the distilled graph rather than its structural diversity alone does not produce it (directional evidence). With this framework and this regularity in hand, the use of LLM causal priors stops being manual trial and error and becomes an empirically verifiable selection problem.

title: A System Architecture for Low Latency Multiprogramming Quantum Computing
abstract: As quantum systems scale, multiprogramming quantum computing (MPQC) provides a practical way to improve device utilization and throughput. However, because quantum executables are device-dependent, non-portable across qubit regions, and highly susceptible to noise and crosstalk, current MPQC pipelines rely on expensive online compilation to co-optimize concurrently running programs. This online step dominates runtime and impedes low-latency deployments for practical, real-world workloads in the future, such as repeatedly invoked quantum neural network (QNN) services. We present FLAMENCO, a fidelity-aware multi-version compilation system that enables independent offline compilation and low-latency multiprogramming at runtime. At the architecture level , the system abstracts devices into compute units to reduce the search space of region allocation. At compile time , it generates diverse executable versions for each program—each bound to a distinct qubit region—allowing dynamic region selection at runtime and overcoming non-portability. At runtime , it employs a lightweight orchestrator that uses post-compilation fidelity metrics to avoid conflicts and mitigate crosstalk, supporting conflict-free co-execution without online co-optimization. Evaluations show that FLAMENCO achieves over 5× runtime speedup in post-scheduling execution while maintaining comparable execution fidelity on common-success workloads. When integrated into existing scheduler-coupled systems, it raises workload-level conflict-free orchestration ratio from 0.183 to 1.000 for HyperQ and from 0.050 to 0.400 for QOS.

title: See the Cost Before You Spend
abstract: AI pricing shouldn’t feel like a surprise at the end of the month. In CasperWasp, the AI panel shows an estimated token cost for each tool alongside your remaining balance—so you can make an informed choice before committing. The estimate can differ slightly from actual billing because usage is based on the provider’s final usage. That transparency is intentional: you should see the cost, not guess it.

title: Title: Self-Modifying Mathematical Proofs
abstract: This paper explores the design of a novel system, termed the 'Recursive Proof Engine,' for automatic generation and refinement of mathematical proofs. Leveraging iterative refinement of axioms and assumptions, the engine integrates concepts of minimal inclusion and constructive validation to achieve rigorous mathematical reasoning. The core mechanism centers around a recursive proof engine that automatically constructs new theorems and systematically refines existing ones, ultimately striving for demonstrable correctness. The system addresses the limitations of traditional proof techniques by embracing automation and formal verification. This work presents a framework for intelligent proof generation, offering a significant advancement in mathematical reasoning and potentially revolutionizing areas requiring precise mathematical validity.

title: Formal Modeling of Emergent Behavior in Complex Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: The study of emergent behavior in complex multi-agent systems presents a significant challenge due to the intricate and often unpredictable interactions among agents. This paper proposes a novel formal mathematical model designed to address this difficulty. The model leverages the principles of cellular automata and stochastic processes to provide a rigorous framework for simulating and analyzing the dynamics of emergent phenomena. Specifically, it incorporates agent interactions, environmental influences, and stochastic elements to accurately represent the complex behaviors observed in such systems. The model's core contribution lies in its ability to predict emergent patterns, offering a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners seeking to understand and control complex systems. The model is defined as follows: Let *N* be the total number of agents in the system. Let *S* be the state space of each agent, where *S* = {s1, s2, ..., sk}, where *k* is the dimensionality of the state space. Let *I(si, sj)* represent the interaction function between agents *i* and *j*, which defines the influence exerted by agent *j* on agent *i* when their states are *si* and *sj*, respectively. Let *E(si)* represent the environmental influence on agent *i* when its state is *si*. Let *σ* be the stochastic element, which introduces randomness into the agent's update rule. The state of agent *i* at time *t+1* is determined by the following equation: *si(t+1)* = *f(si(t), sj(t), E(si(t)), σ)* where *f* is an update function that combines the agent's previous state, the states of its neighbors, environmental influences, and the stochastic element. The system's overall state at time *t+1* is the vector of all agents' states: (*s1(t+1), s2(t+1), ..., sN(t+1)*).

title: Dynamic Adaptive Graph Neural Networks: A Novel Graph Structure Optimization Approach
abstract: This paper presents a novel dynamic adaptive graph neural network (GNN) architecture designed for robust and flexible graph representation learning. Traditional GNNs often rely on static graph structures, limiting their ability to effectively model dynamic graph patterns. Our proposed method introduces a dynamic graph structure adjustment mechanism, enabling the network to adapt its graph topology during training and inference, leading to improved performance and generalization capabilities. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through extensive experiments on diverse graph datasets, showcasing its ability to model complex graph structures with enhanced robustness. The core mechanism focuses on simulating the evolution of graph connectivity through a combination of node and edge weight adjustments, ensuring a dynamically optimized representation.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Neural Networks: A Novel Attention Mechanism
abstract: This paper introduces a dynamic adaptive neural network architecture leveraging a novel attention mechanism. The core principle of this approach is to dynamically adjust the attention weights based on data distribution shifts, enabling a more precise and robust model representation. Traditional attention mechanisms often struggle to maintain optimal performance across diverse datasets. This work presents a mechanism that adapts to changing data distributions, resulting in enhanced model performance and a better understanding of underlying patterns. The proposed architecture aims to address the limitations of static attention models by incorporating a continuous learning and adaptation process. We detail the dynamic weight adjustment strategy and its impact on model accuracy. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential applications and future research directions.

title: Neurotopological Adaptive Neural Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel neural network architecture, termed Neurotopological Adaptive Neural Networks (TANNs), driven by the principles of neurotopology. The core claim is that mimicking the natural, self-organizing topologies of biological neural networks can lead to architectures exhibiting enhanced adaptability, robustness, and learning efficiency. The proposed mechanism involves a dynamic algorithm that adjusts the network's topology – including neuron addition/removal, cluster formation, and synaptic weight modifications – based on local gradient information and connection strengths. Unlike conventional static network topologies, TANNs are designed to evolve and adapt to changing data patterns, mirroring the biological system's inherent plasticity. We outline the key components of the algorithm and discuss its potential benefits across various applications. The primary goal is to explore the feasibility of creating more biologically plausible and effective neural networks.

title: 基于自关联的量子神经网络
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to quantum neural networks (QNNs) leveraging the inherent properties of self-associative quantum systems. Traditional quantum neural networks often struggle with computational complexity and require extensive error correction, limiting their practical applicability. This research proposes a new QNN architecture that utilizes self-associative quantum states to dramatically reduce the number of parameters and enhance the network's ability to learn complex patterns. We demonstrate the superiority of this approach through theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental results on simplified quantum circuits, showcasing significant improvements in both training speed and model capacity compared to existing QNNs. The core mechanism involves dynamically adjusting the entanglement structure within the self-associative system to optimize information flow and propagation, leading to enhanced gradient propagation and reduced computational burden. Further, we explore the potential of this architecture for tackling specific machine learning tasks, including pattern recognition and classification.

title: Probability Space Cyclic Logic Network (PLCN)
abstract: This paper introduces a novel probabilistic space cyclic logic network (PLCN) that offers a significant advancement over traditional logic circuits. PLCNs leverage the power of random variables and probabilistic functions to achieve complex logical operations and automatic expansion capabilities. The core design focuses on a dynamically generated and adjusted set of variables, enabling a flexible and efficient approach to logical computation. This work addresses limitations of conventional logic circuits, particularly in adaptability and the ability to tackle intricate problems. We present a detailed architecture and analysis demonstrating the potential of PLCNs for a wide range of applications.

title: Neural Network Dynamic Topology Learning (NDTL)
abstract: This paper introduces Neural Network Dynamic Topology Learning (NDTL), a novel approach to enhancing neural network performance by directly learning and optimizing its underlying topology. The core claim is that the connection topology of a neural network significantly impacts its performance, necessitating an algorithm capable of autonomous learning and optimization of this structure. NDTL employs a graph convolutional network (GCN) based on unsupervised learning to dynamically adjust both connection weights and topology. The mechanism relies on learning relationships between neurons, allowing for adaptive optimization of the network. Unlike traditional methods that focus solely on weight adjustment, NDTL offers a fundamentally new approach that promises improved performance and efficiency in neural networks. The key contributions are a novel architecture based on GCNs and a methodology for dynamically evolving network topology driven by unsupervised learning. The overall aim is to create more robust and adaptable neural networks capable of tackling complex problems.

title: Probabilistic Inference Based on Biological Neural Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to probabilistic inference utilizing the principles of biological neural networks, specifically drawing inspiration from the structure and function of the hippocampus. Traditional probabilistic modeling struggles with uncertainty and causal reasoning in complex environments. This research introduces a framework that incorporates the key characteristics of biological neural networks – synaptic plasticity, connection patterns, and information encoding – into a probabilistic model. The core mechanism involves simulating these biological features within the model, aiming to enhance its ability to handle complex environments and perform robust inference. The resultant system offers a potentially more efficient and biologically-inspired method for tackling uncertainty and causal reasoning compared to conventional probabilistic approaches. The proposed model leverages recurrent neural network architectures combined with Bayesian inference techniques to achieve this goal. The key contributions include a detailed description of the model architecture, a novel method for incorporating synaptic plasticity, and an evaluation framework for assessing the model's performance in simulated environments.

The resultant system offers a potentially more efficient and biologically-inspired method for tackling uncertainty and causal reasoning compared to conventional probabilistic approaches. The proposed model leverages recurrent neural network architectures combined with Bayesian inference techniques to achieve this goal. The key contributions include a detailed description of the model architecture, a novel method for incorporating synaptic plasticity, and an evaluation framework for assessing the model's performance in simulated environments.

title: Title: Self-Organizing Constraint Propagation for Automated Theorem Proving
abstract: Automated theorem proving is a crucial field in computer science, demanding efficient and scalable methods for verifying mathematical statements. Traditional approaches rely heavily on manual constraint creation, a laborious and time-consuming process. This paper introduces a novel self-organizing constraint propagation system leveraging reinforcement learning to automatically generate and refine constraints. We demonstrate that this approach significantly improves the efficiency and scalability of formal verification by iteratively refining constraints based on the results of theorem proving. The system's architecture incorporates a reinforcement learning agent that continuously adapts to the evolving state of the theorem proving process, resulting in more robust and generalizable constraints. This research aims to provide a paradigm shift in formal verification, moving beyond manual constraint creation towards automated learning.

title: Title: Quantum Information Theory and Geometric Probability
abstract: Quantum Information Theory (QIT) represents a burgeoning field exploring the potential of quantum mechanics to revolutionize computation and communication. A core challenge lies in defining and manipulating probability, traditionally viewed as a statistical concept. This paper proposes a fundamental shift in perspective, formalizing "geometric probability" as a property inherent to quantum systems, and subsequently utilizing this concept to drive the development of novel quantum algorithms. The core claim centers on the idea that geometric probability offers a more direct and powerful pathway to understanding and exploiting quantum phenomena. We investigate the extension of probability to the space of geometric configurations, introducing a new type of probability intrinsically linked to quantum mechanics. This approach moves beyond traditional statistical interpretations, offering a deeper and more mathematically rigorous foundation for quantum information processing. The proposed framework necessitates a re-evaluation of fundamental probability principles, with the potential for significant advancements in algorithm design and the exploration of novel quantum computational paradigms. This work addresses the limitations of current approaches by introducing a geometric perspective that directly reflects the underlying structure of quantum mechanics.

title: Quantum Simulation of Adaptive Parameters
abstract: Quantum simulation offers unprecedented capabilities for modeling complex quantum systems, but traditional methods often struggle with computationally intensive simulations. This paper introduces a novel adaptive parameter adjustment algorithm for quantum simulation, aiming to overcome these limitations by dynamically adjusting simulation parameters based on the results obtained. The core mechanism involves analyzing the simulation trajectory to identify critical parameters, then adjusting these parameters to minimize errors and optimize simulation fidelity. We detail the algorithm's design, the methodology for parameter optimization, and the resulting improvements in accuracy and efficiency compared to existing approaches. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential impact of this approach on various quantum simulation tasks, highlighting its promise for advancing the field.

abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to complex environment simulation leveraging adaptive reinforcement learning. Traditional methods often struggle with the inherent complexity of these environments, requiring extensive tuning and slow learning. Our method dynamically adjusts reinforcement learning parameters to improve the efficiency of environment learning. We introduce a new framework that focuses on maintaining a stable and informative state representation, allowing for faster and more robust adaptation to the environment. The core mechanism involves a continuous parameter optimization process driven by a learned reward function, effectively enhancing the agent's ability to explore and learn in challenging simulated environments. This research addresses a key challenge in complex environment simulation – the difficulty of achieving efficient and effective learning – through a novel integration of adaptive reinforcement learning.

title: Quantum Error Correction: Adaptive Self-Correcting Quantum Computation
abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) is a crucial component of fault-tolerant quantum computation, enabling the reliable execution of complex quantum algorithms. Current QEC protocols often rely on static error correction strategies, limiting the computational capabilities of quantum systems. This paper explores the potential of adaptive self-correcting QEC, proposing a novel architecture based on dynamic parameter adjustment within a quantum error correction network. We demonstrate the benefits of this approach through simulations and analyses, highlighting the ability of the system to dynamically adjust error correction strategies based on quantum state evolution, ultimately leading to improved precision and stability. The core claim addresses the challenge of traditional QEC's limitations – the lack of adaptability – and introduces a mechanism to automate parameter adjustment, thereby unlocking a new era of quantum computing performance.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations and preliminary experiments, showcasing its potential to enhance the performance of machine learning models.

title: What Does an LLM-Agent Leaderboard Rank Actually Compare?
abstract: An LLM-agent leaderboard invites a familiar inference: an agent ranked above another is the better agent. Public evaluation logs may not support that conclusion when systems differ in task mixture, label source, release detail, or cost rule. We study what leaderboard scores estimate and when they justify pairwise superiority conclusions. Our estimand-aware pairwise procedure states the comparison target and measurement source, checks common support, and evaluates the supported difference using a stated uncertainty rule and practical margin. Controlled checks evaluate the decision labels under known finite-sample conditions and show why uncertainty must be included when judging sensitivity to target reweighting. Across SWE-bench, AgentRewardBench, and tau2-bench, close rank differences are often unresolved; proxy labels and utility rules can also change which system is selected. DataAgentBench and Open Agent show what remains estimable from coarser public records. A leaderboard score summarizes a released evaluation, whereas a fine-grained superiority claim additionally depends on the estimand and uncertainty rule used to interpret the difference.

title: Copyright Protection of AI-Generated Works: Challenges and Emerging Legal Approaches
abstract: The quick development of AI (artificial intelligence), especially the technology of generative AI, has dramatically changed the way of creation, distribution, publishing, and consumption of creative and intellectual works. AI systems have gained the ability to create literature, art pieces, music, software, photos, designs, and other creative works either with minimal human intervention or to various extents. On one hand, they have provided opportunities for innovations, but on the other hand, they have created challenges for such concepts as authorship, originality, infringement, ownership, and copyright protection. Copyright Protection of AI-Generated Works: Challenges and Emerging Legal Approaches discusses the controversial relationship between copyright laws and artificial intelligence. Traditionally, copyright systems were designed in the context that creative works are created by human authors. Thus, the appearance of AI-generated and AI-assisted works has opened many questions about whether or not they can be protected by copyright laws, about their authors or owners, and about the extent of human involvement and creativity. The book critically analyzes the above issues through an examination of Indian and international laws and regulations. In particular, attention is paid to the Indian Copyright Act, 1957; the notion of originality and authorship; copyright infringement in connection with the use of AI for learning and generation; licensing and compensation; protection of creators' rights. In addition, the book studies developments on the international level through the Berne Convention; TRIPS Agreement; WIPO treaties; copyright and AI regulation in the European Union; human-authorship approach in the USA; computer-generated works in the UK. Using comparative legal analysis, case-law review, policies, and emerging approaches to regulation, the book aims at identifying shortcomings in current copyright law and exploring potential ways to solve this problem. The author poses a question of whether current copyright law provides sufficient means for regulating the issue of AI-generated creativity or whether new tools of legislation, licensing, transparency requirement, collective management or sui generis solutions should be developed. The book is addressed to researchers, academics, legal practitioners, policy-makers, students, IT professionals and everyone who wants to find out more about this rapidly growing legal field of artificial intelligence and copyright. It is hoped that this publication would make a valuable contribution to the academic and policy debates in this sphere and help create a balanced copyright framework that would ensure both technological innovation and human creativity and authorship.

title: From National Data to Local Evaluation: Benchmarking Machine Learning Models for Perioperative Risk Prediction
abstract: Abstract Whether newer modeling approaches improve perioperative risk prediction is unclear. Holding 73 prespecified preoperative variables fixed — 69 observed and used as tabular inputs, all 73 serialized to text — we benchmarked six tabular model families and three pretrained clinical text-encoder embedding classifiers for four 30-day outcomes, training on 4,995,670 ACS NSQIP cases (2018–2022) and testing temporally on 963,565 cases (2024). The FT-Transformer led or tied on AUROC for all four outcomes (0.755–0.955), exceeding logistic regression by only 0.009–0.030; the three encoders fell 0.005–0.009 short of the best tabular model and spanned 0.003 or less. On identical cases the ACS NSQIP Surgical Risk Calculator matched the best model for mortality but trailed for any complication. Rankings changed under AUPRC and did not hold in a 3,490-case single-institution deployment check, not independent of the PUF. Once the predictor set is fixed, architecture and encoder choice move discrimination little.

title: Online Resource 1: Evidence-Mapping, Screening and Claim-Audit Workbook for Banking Conversational AI

Evidence-access depth is recorded separately from each publication’s contribution to the synthesis.The workbook supports methodological transparency, traceability and reproducibility. It does not contain proprietary banking information, customer records or personal financial data.

title: Dynamic Information Theory: Entropy Generation Model
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic information theory model based on the principles of information theory. The core idea is to dynamically adjust the entropy distribution of a dataset based on its evolving information content. This adaptation allows the model to achieve superior data compression and storage efficiency, particularly in scenarios involving dynamic data. The model leverages a learning mechanism to continuously refine the entropy distribution, ensuring optimal performance across various data types. We present a comprehensive implementation of the model, demonstrating its effectiveness through simulations and preliminary experiments. The research explores the potential of this approach to address limitations of existing entropy generation methods.

title: 基于自适应的概率空间搜索算法
abstract: The development of efficient search algorithms is crucial for various domains, particularly those dealing with high-dimensional and complex data. Traditional search methods often rely on static strategies, which can be inadequate when faced with intricate data characteristics. This paper introduces a novel approach – a dynamic probability space search algorithm – that leverages probabilistic space adjustment to enhance search efficiency, particularly within high-dimensional scenarios. This algorithm dynamically adjusts parameters within the probability space during the search process, offering a significant improvement over static methods. The core mechanism revolves around simulating the search process and dynamically adjusting the probability distribution within the space. This adaptive strategy is designed to address the limitations of conventional search algorithms.

title: Quantum Entanglement as a Logical Computation Model
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a perplexing phenomenon where two or more particles become linked in such a way that they share the same fate, presents a tantalizing prospect for advanced computation. This paper explores the potential of utilizing quantum entanglement to construct a logical computation model, leveraging its unique properties for parallel processing and complex operations. We propose a novel quantum algorithm predicated on this model, aiming to revolutionize traditional computational approaches. The core of this work lies in a detailed architectural design of the entanglement-based logic engine, outlining the fundamental operations and potential applications. The study critically examines the theoretical implications of this approach, focusing on the advantages over existing quantum computing paradigms. We propose a new approach to quantum algorithm development based on entanglement as the foundation.

title: Hyperdimensional Categorical Networks
abstract: Hyperdimensional Categorical Networks (HCNs) propose a novel approach to pattern recognition by leveraging the strengths of hyperdimensional representations and categorical learning. The core concept involves mapping data into a high-dimensional space, typically 128 dimensions or more, and then training a network where each node represents a distinct category. Learning is driven by minimizing the distance between the node's hyperdimensional representation and the input data, utilizing a categorical loss function that explicitly encourages distinct category representations. This architecture significantly enhances pattern recognition and generalization capabilities compared to traditional methods. The key innovation lies in the synergistic combination of these two techniques, offering a computationally efficient and robust solution for complex data analysis. The presented framework demonstrates improved performance across a range of pattern recognition tasks, highlighting its potential for applications in areas such as anomaly detection, sensor data analysis, and bioinformatics. ---

title: Adaptive Metric Learning for Graph Embedding
abstract: Graph embedding techniques have become increasingly prevalent in various domains, including social network analysis, drug discovery, and recommendation systems. A fundamental limitation of many existing approaches is their reliance on fixed metrics to define node similarity and distance. These fixed metrics often fail to capture the nuanced relationships within complex graphs, leading to suboptimal embeddings. This paper proposes a novel framework for adaptive metric learning, which dynamically adjusts the embedding space based on the specific graph structure and the task at hand. The core idea is to train a metric learning model that learns to align nodes based on their contextual relationships, continuously refining the embedding space. We introduce a framework utilizing a contrastive loss function and a differentiable graph neural network (GNN) architecture to achieve adaptive graph embeddings. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms traditional graph embedding methods in several benchmark datasets, highlighting the effectiveness of adaptive metric learning for capturing complex graph structures.

What this is. A standalone theory draft (v0.3, 7 September 2026) in the Human–AI Readout Programme on effort and retry under stochastic, other-controlled, and adaptive worlds. It keeps Effort Under Stochastic and Other-Controlled Worlds v0.1 as its anchor and v0.2 as its mathematical scaffold; v0.3 is an adversarial elevation, not a replacement. title: Adaptive Symmetry Breaking in Deep Learning
abstract: Deep neural networks, despite their success in various domains, frequently suffer from issues related to learning efficiency and generalization capabilities. A significant underlying cause of these problems is the presence of symmetries within the network's learned representations. These symmetries lead to redundant computations and hinder the network's ability to capture truly novel and informative features. This paper proposes a novel approach to address this issue: Adaptive Symmetry Breaking (ASB). The ASB module is dynamically trained within the deep learning architecture to identify and actively disrupt these learned symmetries. This is achieved through controlled noise injection and gradient manipulation, encouraging the network to explore a wider range of representations. The core claim of this work is that a proactive, learned symmetry breaking mechanism, unlike traditional fixed architectural constraints, significantly improves the learning process and enhances the generalization performance of deep neural networks. The theoretical framework outlines the symmetry detection process and the adaptive noise injection strategy, represented as follows: Let *S* represent the set of learned weights in a neural network layer. The symmetry detection function, *D(S)*, measures the degree of symmetry within *S*. The symmetry breaking module then applies a controlled noise *ε* to the weights, resulting in: *S' = S + ε* The magnitude of the noise, *ε*, is adaptively determined based on the output of the symmetry detection function *D(S)*. The loss function is modified to incorporate the symmetry breaking term: *L = L_original + λ * D(S)* where *λ* is a hyperparameter controlling the strength of the symmetry breaking.

title: Causal Discovery via Bayesian Inference on Dynamic Bayesian Networks
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to causal discovery within dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs). The core challenge in inferring causal relationships from time-varying data lies in the complexities introduced by confounding factors and intricate temporal dependencies. This research develops a Bayesian inference framework tailored explicitly for DBNs, incorporating mechanisms to model these temporal aspects and mitigate confounding through a layered strategy combining prior knowledge and data-driven learning. The proposed framework aims to provide a robust and interpretable solution for uncovering causal structures within dynamic systems, addressing a significant gap in current causal discovery methodologies. The key innovations lie in the dynamic updating of the Bayesian network structure and parameters, as well as the integration of techniques for handling spurious correlations. The framework is designed to improve the accuracy and reliability of causal inferences, particularly in scenarios where data is inherently noisy and subject to temporal variations. This work contributes to the field by offering a more principled and effective approach to causal discovery in dynamic environments.

title: Based on Quantum Mechanics Simulation of Neurons Model (QMNN)
abstract: This paper introduces the Quantum Mechanics Simulation of Neurons Model (QMNN), a novel approach to simulating neuronal behavior based on fundamental principles of quantum mechanics. Traditional artificial neural networks (ANNs) often struggle to accurately replicate the complex dynamics observed in biological neurons due to their reliance on classical computational methods. QMNN leverages concepts such as superposition and entanglement, key features of quantum mechanics, to represent neuronal states and interactions. The model employs a discrete quantum system, where neuronal activity is represented by quantum states, allowing for inherent parallelism and potentially capturing phenomena currently inaccessible to classical neural simulations. This work details the core concepts of QMNN, outlining its mathematical formulation, key components, and potential advantages over conventional ANN approaches. We present a simplified model of a single neuron utilizing a quantum bit (qubit) to represent its state. The model's equations reflect the Schrödinger equation and the evolution of quantum states under influence of external stimuli. The simulation explores scenarios demonstrating the potential for increased computational efficiency and the ability to model phenomena like quantum coherence within neuronal networks. Further research will focus on scaling the model to multi-neuron networks and investigating the model's applicability to various neurological conditions.
